title: Opuscula theologica et polemica
author: Maximus the Confessor
source_text:
⟦q1.1|1⟧ [0009] ΤΟΥ ΕΝ ΑΓΙΟΙΣ ΠΑΤΡΟΣ ΗΜΩΝ ΜΑΞΙΜΟΥ ΤΟΥ ΟΜΟΛΟΓΗΤΟΥ ΠΡΟΣ ΜΑΡΙΝΟΝ ΤΟΝ ΟΣΙΩΤΑΤΟΝ ΠΡΕΣΒΥΤΕΡΟΝ. [bid:c9a]Σκοπὸν θέμενος σαυτῷ τὴν πανύμνητον πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν στείλασθαι φιλίαν, θεοτίμητε Πάτερ, εὐτάκτως πρὸς αὐτὴν [n: Tur. αὐτὸν, ut et Dufr. f.] διανύεις τὸν δρόμον. ⟦q1.1|2⟧ Λόγῳ μὲν πρὸς ἀρετῆς γένεσιν τὴν τῶν ὄντων φύσιν περιγράφων · νῷ δὲ, πρὸς ἀπλανοῦς ἑνώσεως [γνώσεως] σύστασιν, παντὸς αἰῶνος καὶ χρόνου περιορίζων τὴν κίνησιν· αἷς θερμότερος ὁ τοῦ Θεοῦ συνεισέρχεται πόθος· τῇ τε ἀπειρίᾳ συμπαρεκτείνων σου τοῦ ποθοῦντος τὴν κίνησιν· καὶ τῷ ἀκαταλήπτῳ τοῦ ποθουμένου, τὴν ἔφεσίν σοι ποιῶν ἀκατάληπτον· ἧς τέλος αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ Θεός· πόθου τοῖς ἀξίοις γινόμενος πλήρωσις, ὡς ἀπόλαυσις ἀγαθῶν αὐθυπόστατος· ἧς μόνην τὴν πεῖραν οἶδε κατάληψιν ὁ λόγος, οἷα σαφῶς ὑπὲρ νόησιν τυγχάνουσαν, ἕνωσιν, ὡς μηδενὶ τύπῳ νοερῷ καθοτιοῦν ὑποπιπτούσης. ⟦q1.1|3⟧ Διὰ τοῦτο, τοῦ μὲν λόγου [bid:c9b]σοι γέγονε πρόσωπον ὁ βίος· τοῦ δὲ βίου φύσις, [0012] [bid:c12a]ὁ λόγος· τὸν καινὸν ἀληθῶς κατὰ Χριστὸν ὑπογράφοντες ἄνθρωπον· εὐμιμήτως φέροντα τοῦ κτίσαντος Θεοῦ τὴν εἰκόνα καὶ τὴν ὁμοίωσιν· ἅστινας ὑποληπτέον νῦν τὴν ἀλήθειαν καὶ τὴν ἀγαθότητα· τὴν μὲν θεωρίας· τὴν δὲ, πράξεως τέλος ὑπάρχουσαν· καὶ τὴν μέν, ψεύδους· τὴν δὲ, πονηρίας ἀντίἘντεῦθέν σοι τῇ κατορθώσει τῶν ἀρετῶν, ἡ τῶν θείων συνήφθη δογμάτων κατάληψις· τῷ τε πλήθει τῆς γνώσεως, καὶ τῇ δυνάμει συνεχομένη τῆς ἀποδείξεως· καθ᾿ ἣν, τὸ πρός τινων οὐκ ἠκριβωμένως περὶ θελημάτων προταθὲν διαγνοὺς, καὶ παρωσάμενος, [bid:c12b]ταυτὸν ἀλλήλοις εἶναι φαμένων θέλημα καὶ βούλησιν, καὶ βουλὴν, καὶ προαίρεσιν καὶ γνώμην· ἐξουσίαν τε καὶ δόξαν καὶ φρόνησιν, μόνοις ἀλλήλων, διαφέροντα τοῖς ὀνόμασι· τοῦ τε Θεοῦ καὶ τῶν ἁγίων ἓν θέλημα γενήσεσθαι· καὶ διὰ τοῦτο βεβαιουμένων τὸν Χριστὸν ἓν θέλημα προαιρετικὸν ἔχειν καὶ διατεινομένων· οὐκ ἠρκέσθης σαυτῷ πρὸς τὴν τοῦ καλῶς κριθέντος βεβαίωσιν, διὰ τὴν σύντροφον πτωχείαν τοῦ πνεύματος· ἀλλὰ κἀμὲ τὸν ἰδιωτείᾳ συντεθραμμένον σύμψηφον λαβεῖν τῶν ἐγνωσμένων σοι καλῶς κατηξίωσας. ⟦q1.1|4⟧ Ὅπερ ποιήσων ἥκω· κἂν προπετές· τῷ τῆς εὐπειθείας μισθῷ νενικημένος. ⟦q1.1|5⟧ Ἑκάστου δὲ τούτων καθ᾿ εἱρμὸν τὴν γραφὴν ποιήσομαι σύντομον, καὶ οἷον ὁριστικήν· οὐκ ἐμοὺς ἐγχαράττων λόγους· πῶς γὰρ, ὁ τούτων πενόμενος, [bid:c12c]ἀλλὰ τοὺς περὶ τούτων ἄλλοις πονηθέντας ἐρανισάμενος, ἵνα γνῶμεν ὡς ἀμφοῖν διαφέρουσιν ἀλλήλων ταῦτα· λέγω δὲ κλήσει καὶ πράγματι. ⟦q1.1|6⟧ Περὶ φυσικοῦ θελήματος, ἤγουν θελήσεως. ⟦q1.1|7⟧ Θέλημά φασιν εἶναι φυσικὸν, ἤγουν θέλησιν, δύναμιν τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν ὄντος ὀρεκτικήν· καὶ τῶν οὐσιωδῶς τῇ φύσει προσόντων συνεκτικὴν πάντων ἰδιωμάτων. ⟦q1.1|8⟧ Τούτῳ γὰρ συνεχομένη φυσικῶς ἡ οὐσία, τοῦ τε εἶναι καὶ ζῇν καὶ κινεῖσθαι κατ᾿ αἴσθησίν τε καὶ νοῦν ὀρέγεται, τῆς οἰκείας ἐφιεμένη φυσικῆς [bid:c12d]καὶ πλήρους ὀντότητος. ⟦q1.1|9⟧ Θελητικὴ γὰρ ἑαυτῆς, καὶ τῶν ὅσα σύστασιν αὐτῆς ποιεῖσθαι πέφυκε, καθέστηκεν ἡ φύσις· τῷ τοῦ εἶναι αὐτῆς λόγῳ, καθ᾿ ὃν ἔστι τε καὶ γέγονεν ὀρεκτικῶς ἐπηρτημένη. ⟦q1.1|10⟧ Διόπερ [0013] [bid:c13a]ἕτεροι τοῦτο τὸ φυσικὸν ὁριζόμενοι· θέλημά φασιν εἶναι, ὄρεξιν λογικήν τε καὶ ζωτικήν· τὴν δὲ προαίρεσιν, ὄρεξιν βουλευτικὴν τῶν ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν. ⟦q1.1|11⟧ Οὐκ ἔστιν οὖν προαίρεσις ἡ θέλησις· εἴπερ ἡ μὲν θέλησις ἁπλῆ τις ὄρεξίς ἐστι, λογική τε καὶ ζωτική· ἡ δὲ προαίρεσις, ὀρέξεως καὶ βουλῆς καὶ κρίσεως σύνοδος. ⟦q1.1|12⟧ Ὁρεγόμενοι γὰρ πρότερον βουλευόμεθα· καὶ βουλευσάμενοι, κρίνομεν· καὶ κρίναντες, προαιρούμεθα τοῦ χείρονος τὸ δειχθὲν ἐκ τῆς κρίσεως κρεῖττον· καὶ ἡ μὲν, μόνον ἤρτηται τῶν φυσικῶν· ἡ δὲ, μόνων τῶν ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν, καὶ δι᾿ ἡμῶν γίνεσθαι δυναμένων. ⟦q1.1|13⟧ Οὐκ ἔστιν οὖν θέλησις ἡ προαίρεσις. [bid:c13b]Περὶ βουλήσεως. ⟦q1.1|14⟧ Ἀλλ᾿ οὔτε βούλησίς ἐστιν ἡ προαίρεσις. ⟦q1.1|15⟧ Βούλησις μὲν γάρ ἐστιν ὄρεξις φανταστικὴ τῶν ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν καὶ οὐκ ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν· τουτέστι μόνῃ τῇ διανοίᾳ μορφουμένη. ⟦q1.1|16⟧ Ἡ δὲ ὄρεξις φανταστικὴ, μόνης ἐστὶ τῆς διανοητικῆς δυνάμεως ἄνευ τοῦ βουλευτικοῦ λόγου. τῶν ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν· ἢ ποιὰ φυσικὴ θέλησις. ⟦q1.1|17⟧ Ἡ δὲ προαίρεσις, ὄρεξις βουλευτικὴ τῶν ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν πρακτῶν. ⟦q1.1|18⟧ Ἤρκει μὲν οὖν καὶ μόνος ὁ τῆς ὑπογραφῆς λόγος, δείξας τὴν τούτων διαφορὰν, παῦσαι φιλονεικίας τοὺς περιττῶς φιλολογοῦντας· καὶ τοῖς καλῶς ἐγνωσμένοις, οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅπως εὐφήμως εἰπεῖν, σαφῶς ἀντιλέγοντας. ⟦q1.1|19⟧ Ἐπειδὴ δὲ ποθοῦσί πως οἱ φιλοπευστοῦντες διὰ πλειόνων ἐπιστῆναι τοῖς ζητουμένοις, ἐροῦμεν καὶ ἄλλως· Φασὶν οἱ περὶ τούτων διειληφότες· Οὐ πᾶσιν οἷς ἁρμόζει τὸ προαιρεῖσθαι, πάντως [bid:c13c]ἁρμόζειν καὶ τὸ βούλεσθαι. ⟦q1.1|20⟧ Βούλεσθαι μὲν γὰρ ὑγιαίνειν καὶ πλουτεῖν καὶ ἀθανατισθῆναί φαμεν· προαιρεῖσθαι δὲ πλουτεῖν καὶ ὑγιαίνειν καὶ ἀθανατισθῆναι, οὐ λέγομεν· ἐπειδὴ ἡ μὲν βούλησις, καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν δυνατῶν καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀδυνάτων ἐστίν· ἡ δὲ προαίρεσις, ἐπὶ μόνων δυνατῶν, καὶ δι᾿ ἡμῶν γενέσθαι δυναμένων. ⟦q1.1|21⟧ Καὶ πάλιν, ἡ μὲν βούλησις, τοῦ τέλους ἐστίν· ἡ δὲ προαίρεσις, τῶν πρὸς τὸ τέλος. ⟦q1.1|22⟧ Τέλος οὖν εἶναί φασι τὸ βουλητόν· οἷον, τὴν ὑγίειαν· πρὸς τὸ τέλος δὲ, τὸ βουλευτόν· οἷον, τὸν τῆς ὑγιείας τόπον. ⟦q1.1|23⟧ Τὴν αὐτὴν οὖν ἀναλογίαν ἣν ἔχει τὸ βουλητὸν πρὸς τὸ βουλευτὸν, ἔχειν τὴν βούλησίν φασι [0016] [bid:c16a]πρὸς τὴν προαίρεσιν· εἴπερ ταῦτα μόνα προαιρούμεθα, ἃ δι᾿ ἡμῶν οἰόμεθα δύνασθαι γενέσθαι. ⟦q1.1|24⟧ Βουλόμεθα δὲ καὶ τὰ μὴ δι᾿ ἡμῶν οἷά τε γενέσθαι. ⟦q1.1|25⟧ Δέδεικται τοίνυν, ὡς οὐδὲ βούλησίς ἐστιν ἡ προαίρεσις· δειχθήσεται δὲ πάλιν, ὡς οὔτε βούλευσίς ἐστιν ἤγουν βουλή. ⟦q1.1|26⟧ Περὶ βουλῆς ἤγουν βουλεύσεως. ⟦q1.1|27⟧ Τὴν βουλὴν ἤγουν βούλευσιν εἶναί φασιν ὄρεξιν [bid:c16b]ζητητικὴν περί τι τῶν ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν πρακτῶν γινομένην. ⟦q1.1|28⟧ Προαιρετὸν δὲ, τὸ ἐκ τῆς βουλῆς κριθέν. ⟦q1.1|29⟧ Δῆλον οὖν ἐντεῦθεν, ὡς ἡ μὲν βούλευσις, ἐπὶ τοῖς ἔτι ζητοῦμένοις ἐστίν· ἡ δὲ προαίρεσις, ἐπὶ τοῖς ἤδη προκεκριμένοις. ⟦q1.1|30⟧ Καὶ δῆλον, οὐκ ἐκ μόνου τοῦ ὁρισμοῦ, ἀλλὰ κἀκ τῆς ἐτυμολογίας [n: in Ethic. c. 2.]. ⟦q1.1|31⟧ Προαιρετὸν γάρ ἐστι, τὸ ἕτερον πρὸ ἑτέρου αἱρετόν. ⟦q1.1|32⟧ Οὐδεὶς δὲ προκρίνει τι, μὴ βουλευσάμενος· οὐδὲ αἱρεῖται μὴ κρίνας. ⟦q1.1|33⟧ Οὐκ ἔστιν οὖν βουλὴ, τουτέστι βούλευσις, ἡ προαίρεσις. ⟦q1.1|34⟧ Περὶ προαιρέσεως. ⟦q1.1|35⟧ «Προαίρεσιν [n: Nemes. c. 33.] εἶναί φασιν ὄρεξιν βουλευτικὴν τῶν [bid:c16c]ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν πρακτῶν. ⟦q1.1|36⟧ Μικτὸν γάρ τι, καὶ πολλοῖς σύγκρατον ἡ προαίρεσις· ἐξ ὀρέξεως καὶ βουλῆς συγκειμένη καὶ κρίσεως. ⟦q1.1|37⟧ Οὐδέτερον γὰρ τούτων ὑπάρχει καθ᾿ αὐτὸ θεωρούμενον ἡ προαίρεσις· οὔτε γὰρ μόνον ὄρεξις καθ᾿ αὐτὴν, οὔτε βουλὴ, οὔτε κρίσις· ἀλλὰ ἐκ τούτων σύγκρατος, καθὼς ὁ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς ἄνθρωπος ἐκ ψυχῆς καὶ σώματος σύνθετος. ⟦q1.1|38⟧ Ἐπειδὴ τότε προαίρεσις, καὶ προαιρετὸν γίνεται, τὸ προκριθὲν ἐκ τῆς βουλῆς, περὶ οὗ ἡ προαίρεσις, ὅταν προσλάβῃ τὴν ὄρεξιν. ⟦q1.1|39⟧ Ἀναγκαίως οὖν ἡ προαίρεσις περὶ ταῦτά ἐστι μετὰ τὴν κρίσιν, περὶ ἃ ἡ βουλὴ πρὸ τῆς κρίσεως. ⟦q1.1|40⟧ Ἐκεῖνα γὰρ προαιρούμεθα, περὶ [bid:c16d]ὧν βουλευόμεθα. ⟦q1.1|41⟧ Περὶ τίνων βουλευόμεθα. ⟦q1.1|42⟧ Βουλευόμεθα δὲ περὶ τῶν ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν καὶ δι᾿ ἡμῶν γίνεσθαι δυναμένων· καὶ ἄδηλον ἐχόντων τὸ τέλος. ⟦q1.1|43⟧ Τὸ μὲν οὖν ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν εἴρηται, ἐπειδὴ περὶ τῶν πρακτῶν μόνον βουλευόμεθα. ⟦q1.1|44⟧ Ταῦτα γὰρ ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν· οὐ γὰρ περὶ τῆς αὐθυποστάτου σοφίας. ⟦q1.1|45⟧ Οὔτε γὰρ περὶ Θεοῦ, οὔτε περὶ τῶν ἐξ ἀνάγκης καὶ ἀεὶ ὡσαύτως γινομένων· οἷον [n: κύκλου τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ.] τῆς κυκλικῆς τῶν χρόνων κινήσεως· οὔτε περὶ τῶν οὐκ ἀεὶ μὲν ὄντων, ἀεὶ δὲ ὁμοίως γινομένων, οἷον ἀνατολῆς ἡλίου καὶ δύσεως· οὔτε περὶ τῶν φύσει μὲν, οὐκ ἀεὶ δὲ ὁμοίως γινομένων, [0017] [bid:c17a]ἀλλ᾿ ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πλεῖστον· οἷον, περὶ τοῦ πολιοῦσθαι τὸν ἑξηκοντούτην, ἢ γενειάσκειν τὸν εἰκοσαετῆ· οὔτε περὶ τῶν φύσει μὲν, ἄλλοτε δὲ ἄλλως ἀορίστως γινομένων· οἷον περὶ ὄμβρων καὶ αὐχμῶν καὶ χαλάζης. ⟦q1.1|46⟧ Διὰ ταῦτα μὲν, τὸ ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν, εἴρηται· Τὸ δὲ, Δι᾿ ἡμῶν γίνεσθαι δυναμένων· ἐπειδήπερ οὐ περὶ πάντων ἀνθρώπων [τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων], οὔτε περὶ παντὸς πράγματος βουλευόμεθα· ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ περὶ πάντων τῶν ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν, καὶ δι᾿ ἡμῶν γινομένων· ἀλλὰ δεῖ προσκεῖσθαι, καὶ ἄδηλον ἐχόντων τὸ τέλος. ⟦q1.1|47⟧ Ἐὰν γὰρ ᾗ φανερὸν καὶ ὁμολογούμενον, οὐκ ἔτι περὶ αὐτοῦ βουλευόμεθα· κἂν ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν, καὶ δι᾿ ἡμῶν γίνηται. ⟦q1.1|48⟧ Ἐδείχθη δὲ, ὡς οὐδὲ περὶ τοῦ τέλους, ἀλλὰ περὶ τῶν πρὸς τὸ τέλος, ἡ βουλή. ⟦q1.1|49⟧ Βουλευόμεθα γὰρ οὐ πλουτῆσαι· ἀλλ᾿ ὅπως καὶ δι᾿ ὧν πλουτήσομεν. ⟦q1.1|50⟧ Καὶ συντόμως εἰπεῖν, περὶ τούτων μόνον βοβουλευόμεθα ὧν ἡ πρᾶξις ἐπίσης ἐνδέχεται· ἔστι δὲ [bid:c17b]ἐπίσης ἐνδεχόμενον, ὃ αὐτό τε δυνάμεθα, καὶ τὸ ἀντικείμενον αὐτῷ. ⟦q1.1|51⟧ Εἰ γὰρ μὴ ἀμφότερα ἠδυνάμεθα, οὐκ ἂν περὶ ἀμφοτέρων ἐβουλευόμεθα. ⟦q1.1|52⟧ Περὶ γὰρ τῶν ὁμολογουμένων καὶ φανερῶν, ἢ τῶν ἀδυνάτων, καὶ οὐκ ἐνδεχομένων, οὐδεὶς βουλεύεται. ⟦q1.1|53⟧ Εἰ δὲ τὸ ἕτερον μόνον τῶν ἀντικειμένων ἠδυνάμεθα, τοῦτο μὲν ἦν ὁμολογούμενον, ὡς ἀναμφίβολον· τὸ δὲ ἀντικείμενον, ἀδύνατον. ⟦q1.1|54⟧ Οἷον, ἄρτου καὶ λίθου προκειμένων, οὐδεὶς βουλεύεται ποῖον ποιήσεται βρῶμα· τοῦ μὲν ὁμολογουμένου· τοῦ δὲ σαφῶς ὄντος ἀδυνάτου. ⟦q1.1|55⟧ Ταῦτα γοῦν προαιρούμεθα, τὰ ἐπίσης ἐνδεχόμενα, περὶ ὧν καὶ βουλευόμεθα. [bid:c17c]Περὶ γνώμης. ⟦q1.1|56⟧ Ἀλλ οὔτε γνώμη τίς ἐστιν ἡ προαίρεσις, κἂν οἱ πολλοὶ τοῦτο προχείρως νομίζωσιν· ἀλλὰ γνώμης· εἴπερ τὴν γνώμην εἶναί φασιν ὄρεξιν ἐνδιάθετον τῶν ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν, ἐξ ἧς ἡ προαίρεσις· ἢ διάθεσιν ἐπὶ τοῖς ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν ὀρεκτικῶς βουλευθεῖσι. ⟦q1.1|57⟧ Διατεθεῖσα γὰρ ἡ ὄρεξις τοῖς κριθεῖσιν ἐκ τῆς βουλῆς, γνώμη γέγονε· μεθ᾿ ἣν, ἢ κυριώτερον εἰπεῖν, ἐξ ἧς ἡ προαίρεσις. ⟦q1.1|58⟧ Ἕξεως οὖν πρὸς ἐνέργειαν ἐπέχει λόγον, ἡ γνώμη πρὸς τὴν προαίρεσιν. ⟦q1.1|59⟧ Περὶ ἐξουσίας. ⟦q1.1|60⟧ Ἀλλ᾿ οὔτε ἐξουσία ἐστὶν ἡ προαίρεσις. ⟦q1.1|61⟧ Ἡ μὲν γὰρ προαίρεσις, ὡς πολλάκις ἔφην, ὄρεξίς ἐστι βουλευτικὴ τῶν ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν πρακτῶν· ἡ δὲ ἐξουσία, κυριότης [bid:c17d]ἔννομος τῶν ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν πρακτῶν· ἢ κυριότης ἀκώλυτος τῆς τῶν ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν χρήσεως· ἢ ὄρεξις τῶν ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν ἀδούλωτος. ⟦q1.1|62⟧ Οὐκ ἔστιν οὖν ταυτὸν ἐξουσία καὶ προαίρεσις· εἴπερ κατ᾿ ἐξουσίαν μὲν προαιρούμεθα· οὐκ ἐξουσιάζομεν δὲ κατὰ προαίρεσιν· καὶ ἡ μὲν ἐπιλέγεται μόνον· ἡ δὲ χρᾶται τοῖς ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν, καὶ τοῖς ἐπὶ τοῖς ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν, ἤγουν, προαιρέσει καὶ κρίσει καὶ βουλῇ. ⟦q1.1|63⟧ Κατ᾿ ἐξουσίαν γὰρ βουλευόμεθα, [0020] καὶ κρίνομεν, καὶ προαιρούμεθα, καὶ ὁρμῶμεν, καὶ χρώμεθα τοῖς ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν. ⟦q1.1|64⟧ Περὶ δόξης. ⟦q1.1|65⟧ Ἀλλ᾿ οὔτε δόξα τίς ἐστιν ἡ προαίρεσις. ⟦q1.1|66⟧ Ἡ μὲν γὰρ δόξα διττή· λογική τε, καὶ ἄλογος· ἡ δὲ προαίρεσις τρεπτή. ⟦q1.1|67⟧ Τὴν μὲν οὖν ἄλογον δόξαν εἶναί φασιν, ἁπλῆν γνῶσιν καὶ πρόχειρον· ὡς ὅταν τις πρόφέρῃ δόξαν ἀλλοτρίαν, ἀγνοῶν τὴν αὐτῆς αἰτίαν. ⟦q1.1|68⟧ Οἷον, ἀθάνατον λέγων τὴν ψυχὴν, καὶ μὴ διδοὺς ἀποδεικτικὴν αἰτίαν τῆς ἀθανασίας αὐτῆς Τὴν δὲ λογικὴν δόξαν, γνῶσιν εἶναι λέγουσι, κατὰ ἀποπεράτωσιν [bid:c20b]τῆς διανοίας συνισταμένην· ὡς ὅταν τις λογισάμενός τι, καὶ τὴν αἰτίαν αὐτοῦ ἐπιστημονικῶς ἀποδίδωσι. ⟦q1.1|69⟧ Διάνοια γάρ ἐστιν, ἡ διήκουσα καὶ διαστηματικῶς ἐνεργοῦσα, ἀπὸ προτάσεως ἀρχομένη μέχρι συμπεράσματος. ⟦q1.1|70⟧ Οἷον, προτίθεταί τις δεῖξαι τὴν ψυχὴν ἀθάνατον, καὶ λέγει· Ἐπειδὴ αὐτοκίνητός ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή· τὸ δὲ αὐτοκίνητον, ἀεικίνητον· τὸ δὲ ἀεικίνητον, ἀθάνατον· ⟦q15.18|1⟧ De quibus omnibus miseri, nec sensus apostolice facti sunt sedis; et quod est risu, imo, ut magis proprie dicamus, lamento dignissimum, utpote illorum demonstrotivum audaciae, nec adversus ipsam apostolicam sedem mentiri temere pigritati sunt : sed quasi illius effecti consilii, et veluti quodam ab eo recepto decreto, in suis contextis pro impia Ecthesi actionibus, secum, magnum Honorium acceperant, suæ præsumptionis ostentationem [bid:c143b]ad alios facientes, viri in causa pietatis maximam eminentiam. ⟦q15.18|2⟧ Quis itaque, o famosissime, et qualis, Sophronius hæc et tam atrociter. et per tantum temporis facere his falsiloquis: persuasit? quae hos non rogavit Ecclesia? quis pius et. orthodoxus non supplicavit antistes, cessare illos a propria haeresi clamando et obtestando ? siquidem ultima sua exspirabat sacer Arcadius et spiritum Deo tradebat : sed neque usque ad horam illam eos rogare cessavit.

⟦q15.19|1⟧ Et post pauca.

⟦q15.20|1⟧ Quid autem et divinus Honorius ; quid vero et post. illum Severinus senex : quid denique et is, qui post hunc exstitit, sacer Joannes? ⟦q15.20|2⟧ Porro is qui nunc presidet beatissimus papa, omisit quidquam supplicationi conveniens? ⟦q15.20|3⟧ Nonne Oriens totus et Occidens lacrymas, lamenta, obsecraliones, deprecationes ex aequo, tam Deo per orationes, quam his per epistolas offerebant ? ⟦q15.20|4⟧ Sed Deus quidem horum profecto beatorum virorum fidem admisit, et pro ea vicissitudinem iu sæcula conservavit. ⟦q15.20|5⟧ Illi autem Domini contemnentes inducias, ad conversionem hos benigne cohortantes, et horum egregiorum facta per tot tempora supplicatione torpentes, suæ nequaquam passi sunt cœlestem fidem præferre.

⟦q15.21|1⟧ Post aliqua.

⟦q15.22|1⟧ Divinus ergo magnusque Sophronius tunc Alexandriam veniens, mox ex prima lectione (dederat enim etiam ipsi Cyrus ad retractandum illa novem impietatis capitula) lugubre quiddam et ingens. vociferatus, fontes emittebat. lacrymarum illum fervide obsecrans, supplicans, expostalans, in pavimento ipsius pedibus provolutus, quo nihil horum super ambonem contra catholicam Dei Ecclesiam praedicaret : quippe eum hæc liquido impii essent Apollinarii dogmata. 

⟦q15.23|1⟧ Et paulo post.

⟦q15.24|1⟧ Taliter viri, o mihi præ omnibus reverendum caput, divina Deo perosis insultationibus, et invicem scenicis quodammodo illusionibus lacerabant, et sacratissimum Sophronium tam miserabiliter lamentatum, utpote, contritionem more cujusdam secundi Jeremiæ catholicæ deflentem Ecclesie, tantumque divinorum lapsum bene valde et compatientissime [0144] [bid:c144a]dogmatum deplorantem, nullatenus consolati sunt...

⟦q15.25|1⟧ Et post. nonnulla.

⟦q15.26|1⟧ Si enim Romana sedes. non solum reprobum Pyrrhum, sed et male sentientem et male credentem non nescit, perspicuum profecto est, quia omnis, qui eos, qui Pyrrhum repro baverunt, anathematizat, sedem Romanam, id est, catholicam Ecclesiam anathematizat. ⟦q15.26|2⟧ Omitto enim dicere, quia utique et seipsum, qui talis est, si duntaxat sedi Romanæ communicat, catholicæque Dei Ecclesie. ⟦q15.26|3⟧ Obsecro igitur, benedicte domine mi, praecipere omnibus, ne Pyrrhum sanctissimum vel Almificum nominent. ⟦q15.26|4⟧ Neque enim tale quid sacra regula eum vocari permittit, A cuncta enim cecidit. sanctitate, qui nimirum ab Ecclesia catholica [bid:c144b]sponte prosiliit. ⟦q15.26|5⟧ Non enim fas est illum ex quacungue laude cognominari, qui jam olim damnatus est et abjectus ab apostolica sede Romanæ urbis, ob externæ sensum opinionis, donec ab ea recipiatur conversus ad ipsam; imo ad Dominum Deum nostrum per piam confessionem et orthodoxam fidem, qua sanctificationem recipiat, sanctumque vocabulum.

⟦q15.27|1⟧ Itaque si vult hereticus non esse, neque audire, non isti aut illi satisfaciat ; superfluum quippe hoc et irrationabile est : quia sicut uno contra eum scandalizato omnes scandalizati sunt; ita quoque uno satisfacto, omnes procul dubio satisfiunt. ⟦q15.27|2⟧ Festinet pro omnibus sedi Romanæ satisfacere. ⟦q15.27|3⟧ Hac enim satisfacta, communiter ubique omnes pium hunc. et orthodoxum predicabunt. ⟦q15.27|4⟧ Nam frustra solummodo loquitur, qui mihi similes suadendos putat, et non satisfacit el implorat sanctissimæ Romanorum Ecclesi beatissimam papam, id est, apostolicam sedem, qua ab ipso incarnato Dei Verbo, sed et omnibus sanctis synodis, secundum sacros canones et terminos, universarum, qua in toto terrarum orbe sunt, sanctarum Dei Ecclesiarum in omnihus et per omnia percepit et habet imperium, auctoritatem et potestatem ligandi et solvendi. ⟦q15.27|5⟧ Cum bac enim ligat et solvit eliam in coelo Verbum, quod cœlestibus virtutibus principatur. ⟦q15.27|6⟧ Si enim alios quidem satisfaciendos ducit, et beatissimum Romanum papam nequaquam implorat, simile, quiddam agit ei, qui forte homicidii, vel alterius cujusdam criminis redarguitur, et insontem se, non ei, quisecundum leges judicandi jura sortitus est, exhibere festinat : sed tantum inutiliter et sine lucro aliis et privatis hominibus munditiam monstrare sui satagit actus, qui nullam habeant se solvendi a crimine potestatem.

⟦q15.28|1⟧ Quapropter, benedicte mi domine, adhuc. magis extende præceptionem, quæ bene vobis et secundum placitum Dci visa fuisse dignoscitur, quo nemini licentiam habeat iste quidquam loqui et eloqui dogmatis causa. ⟦q15.28|2⟧ Sed liquido -discite voluntatem hujus abundantius investigantes, si velit. annuere [0145] penitus veritati : et si hoc agere studuerit, et ad id secundum rationem accelerat, hortamini eum suggestionem convenienter facere ad beatissimum papam Romanum : quatenus sic per illius divinam [0146] præceptionem, regulariter, quæ circa ipsum sunt, et decentissime moderetur ad gloriam Dei, et vestræ laudem sublimitatis.

⟦q16.1|1⟧ [0145] ΤΟΥ ΑΓΙΟΥ ΜΑΞΙΜΟΥ Περὶ τῶν δύο τοῦ Χριστοῦ φύσεων.

⟦q16.2|1⟧ αʹ. ⟦q16.2|2⟧ Ὁ Ἄρειος τὰς τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις ὁμολογεῖ· ἀλλὰ τὴν Μονάδα ἀρνεῖται· καὶ οὐ λέγει ὁμοούσιον τὴν ἁγίαν Τριάδα. ⟦q16.2|3⟧ Ὁ δὲ Σαβέλλιος, τὴν Μονάδα ὁμολογεῖ· ἀλλὰ τὴν Τριάδα ἀρνεῖται· τὸν γὰρ αὐτὸν λέγει Πατέρα καὶ Υἱὸν καὶ ἅγιον Πνεῦμα· ἡ δὲ Ἑκκλησία τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ τὴν Μονάδα [n: Fr. καὶ Μονάδα καὶ Τριάδα.] ὁμολογεῖ, καὶ τὴν Τριάδα κηρύττει. ⟦q16.2|4⟧ Ὁ Μακεδόνιος ὅμοια τῷ [bid:c145b]Ἀρείῳ πρεσβεύει· τὸ γὰρ ἅγιον Πνεῦμα, κτίσμα ὑποτίθησιν· ἡ δὲ Ἐκκλησία, ὁμοούσιον τῷ Πατρὶ καὶ τῷ Υἱῷ τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἀνακηρύττει, καὶ Θεὸν πῶς διαβεβαιοῖ. ⟦q16.2|5⟧ Ὁμοίως καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ ἑνὸς τῆς ἀγίας Τριάδος, Νεστόριος τὴν φυσικὴν διαφορὰν λέγει· ἀλλὰ τὴν ἕνωσιν οὐχ ὁμολογεῖ, οὐ γὰρ λέγει ταύτην καθ᾿ ὑπόστασιν γεγονέναι. ⟦q16.2|6⟧ Ὁ δὲ Εὐτυχὴς, τὴν μὲν ἕνωσιν ὁμολογεῖ· τὴν δὲ κατ᾿ οὐσίαν διαφορὰν ἀρνεῖται, καὶ σύγχυσιν τῶν φύσεων εἰσάγει. ⟦q16.2|7⟧ Ἡ δὲ Ἐκκλησία, καὶ τὴν καθ᾿ ὑπόστασιν ἕνωσιν διὰ τὸ ἀδιαίρετον, καὶ τὴν κατ᾿ οὐσίαν διαφορὰν διὰ τὸ ἀσύγχυτον πρεσβεύει.

⟦q16.3|1⟧ βʹ. ⟦q16.3|2⟧ Πῶς ἡ ἄκρα ἕνωσις καὶ ταυτότητα ἔχει, καὶ ἑτερότητα; ⟦q16.3|3⟧ Ἢ ταυτότητα οὐσιῶν καὶ ἑτερότητα προσώπων, καὶ τὸ ἔμπαλιν. ⟦q16.3|4⟧ Οἷον ἐπὶ τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος, [bid:c145c]ταυτότης μέν ἐστιν οὐσίας· ἑτερότης δὲ προσώπων· μίαν γὰρ οὐσίαν ὁμολογοῦμεν· τρεῖς δὲ ὑποστάσεις. ⟦q16.3|5⟧ Ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, ταυτότης μὲν ἐστι προσώπου· ἑτερότης δὲ οὐσιῶν· ἑνὸς γὰρ ὄντος ἀνθρώπου, ἄλλης οὐσίας ἐστὶν ἡ ψυχὴ, καὶ ἄλλης ἡ σάρξ [n: Fr. τὸ σῶμα, ut et Turr.]. ⟦q16.3|6⟧ Ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ Δεσπόπου Χριστοῦ· ταυτότης μέν ἐστι, προσώπου· ἑτερότης δὲ, οὐσιῶν· ἑνὸς γὰρ ὄντος προσώπου, ἤτοι ὑποστάσεως, ἑτέρας οὐσίας [0148] [bid:c148a]ἐστὶν ἡ θεότης, καὶ ἑτέρας ἡ ἀνθρωπότης. ⟦q16.3|7⟧ Ὥσπερ γὰρ ἀδύνατον τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος ὁμολογεῖν μὲν τὴν ἕνωσιν, μὴ ἐκφωνεῖν δὲ τὴν διαφοράν· οὔτως ἀνάγκη πᾶσα ἐπὶ τοῦ ἑνὸς τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος, καὶ τὴν ἕνωσιν καὶ τὴν διαφορὰν κηρύττειν.

⟦q16.4|1⟧ γʹ. ⟦q16.4|2⟧ Ὥσπερ γὰρ οὐ διὰ τῶν αὐτῶν σημαίνεται λέξεων, ἤ τε διαφορὰ καὶ ἡ ἕνωσις ἐπὶ τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος· ἀλλὰ διὰ τοῦ μὲν λέγειν τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις, ἡ διαφορά· διὰ τοῦ ὁμολογεῖν δὲ μίαν οὐσίαν, ἡ ἕνωσις ὁμολογεῖται· οὕτω καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ ἑνὸς τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος· διὰ μὲν τοῦ γνωρίζειν τὰς δύο φύσεις, ἡ διαφορά· διὰ δὲ τοῦ κηρύττειν μίαν ὑπόστασιν σύνθετον, ἡ ἕνωσις ὁμολογεῖται. [bid:c148b]δʹ. ⟦q16.4|3⟧ Ὥσπερ γὰρ Ἄρειον ἀναθεματίζομεν, οὐχ ὡς κηρύττοντα [n: Tilian. et Fr. οὐ κηρύττον: et sic in aliis; Turr. deest negans particula.] ἐπὶ τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος τὴν καθ᾿ ὑπόστασιν διαφοράν· ἀλλ᾿ ὡς μὴ λέγοντα τὴν φυσικὴν ἕνωσιν· οὕτω καὶ Νεστόριον ἀναθεματίζομεν, οὐχ ὡς γνωρίζοντα τὴν φυσικὴν διαφορὰν ἐπὶ τοῦ Χριστοῦ· ἀλλ᾿ ὡς μὴ λέγοντα τὴν καθ᾿ ὑπόστασιν ἕνωσιν.

⟦q16.5|1⟧ εʹ. ⟦q16.5|2⟧ Ὥσπερ Σαβέλλιον ἀναθεματίζομεν, οὐχ ὡς κηρύττοντα ἐπὶ τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος τὴν φυσικὴν ἕνωσιν· ἀλλ᾿ ὡς μὴ λέγοντα τὴν καθ᾿ ὑπόστασιν διαφοράν· οὕτως Εὐτυχέα ἀναθεματίζομεν, οὐχ ὡς μὴ λέγοντα τὴν καθ᾿ ὑπόστασιν ἕνωσιν ἐπὶ τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἀλλ᾿ ὡς μὴ γνωρίζοντα τὴν φυσικὴν διαφοράν.

⟦q16.6|1⟧ ϛʹ. ⟦q16.6|2⟧ Τὴν καθ᾿ ὑπόστασιν διαφορὰν ἐπὶ τῆς ἀγίας [bid:c148c]Τριάδος, καὶ τὴν φυσικὴν διαφορὰν ἐπὶ τοῦ ἑνὸς τῆς ἀγίας Τριάδος, οὐκ ἐν αἰσθήσει χρὴ λέγειν, ἀλλὰ νοῆσαι τοῖς τῆς διανοίας ὄμμασιν. ⟦q16.6|3⟧ Καὶ πῶς, ἐπὶ μὲν τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος ἐκφωνεῖτε τὰς τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις διὰ τὴν καθ᾿ ὑπόστασιν διαφοράν· ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ ἑνὸς τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος οὐκ ἐκφωνεῖτε δύο φύσεις ἐν μιᾷ ὑποστάσει, διὰ τὴν φυσικὴν διαφοράν;

⟦q16.7|1⟧ ζʹ. ⟦q16.7|2⟧ Ὥσπερ διὰ τὸ ὁμοούσιον τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος, μίαν οὐσίαν· καὶ διὰ τὸ ἑτεροὑπόστατον τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις λέγεις· οὕτω διὰ τὸ ἑτεροούσιον τοῦ Λόγου καὶ τῆς σαρκὸς, δύο οὐσίας· καὶ διὰ τὸ μὴ ἰδιοῦπόστατον, μίαν ὑπόστασιν λέγε.

⟦q16.8|1⟧ [bid:c148d]ηʹ. ⟦q16.8|2⟧ Ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τῆς ἀγίας Τριάδος τὴν μίαν οὐσίαν, οὐκ ἐπὶ συγχύσει τῶν τριῶν ὑποστάσεων λέγομεν· οὔτε τὰς τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις ἐπὶ ἀναιρέσει τῆς μιᾶς οὐσίας· οὕτως ἐπὶ τοῦ ἑνὸς τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος, [0149] [bid:c149a]τὴν μίαν ὑπόστασιν, οὐκ ἐπὶ συγχύσει τῶν δύο φύσεων αὐτοῦ λέγομεν· οὔτε τὰς δύο φύσεις, ἐπὶ διαιρέσει τῆς μιᾶς ὑποστάσεως.

⟦q16.9|1⟧ θʹ. ⟦q16.9|2⟧ Ὁ μὴ λέγων ἐπὶ Χριστοῦ διὰ τὴν τῶν φύσεων διαφορὰν τὴν καθ᾿ ὑπόστασιν ἕνωσιν, Νεστοριανός ἐστι· καὶ ὁ μὴ λέγων ἐν τῇ καθ᾿ ὑπόστασιν ἑνώσει τὴν φυσικὴν διαφορὰν, Εὐτυχιανιστής ἐστι· ὁ δὲ καὶ τὴν καθ᾿ ὑπόστασιν ἕνωσιν, καὶ τὴν φυσικὴν διαφορὰν κηρύττων ἐπὶ τοῦ ἑνὸς τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος, τὴν βασιλικὴν καὶ ἀμώμητον πίστιν κρατεῖ.

⟦q16.10|1⟧ ιʹ. ⟦q16.10|2⟧ Ὁ τοίνυν λέγων καὶ διαφορὰν καὶ ἕνωσιν ἐπὶ τοῦ Χριστοῦ, οὔτε τὴν διαφορὰν ἀναιρεῖ, οὔτε τὴν ἕνωσιν συγχέει. ⟦q16.10|3⟧ Καὶ γὰρ ὁ θεῖος Κύριλλος [n: Tilian. ὁ μακάριος. Fr. et Turr. καὶ γὰρ Κύριλλος] ἀναθεματίζει τοὺς διὰ τὴν διαφορὰν ἀναιροῦντας τὴν καθ᾿ [bid:c149b]ὑπόστασιν ἕνωσιν· καὶ ἡ οἰκουμενικὴ σύνοδος ἀναθεματίζει τοὺς διὰ τὴν καθ᾿ ὑπόστασιν ἕνωσιν ἀναιροῦντας τὴν φυσικὴν διαφορὰν ἐπὶ τοῦ ἑνὸς τῆς ἀγίας Τριάδος.

⟦q16.11|1⟧ ΜΑΞΙΜΟΥ ΤΟΥ ΟΜΟΛΟΓΗΤΟΥ. ⟦q16.11|2⟧ Ὅροι διάφοροι. ⟦q16.11|3⟧ Οὐσία καὶ φύσις, ταυτόν· ἄμφω γὰρ κοινὸν καὶ καθόλου, ὡς κατὰ πολλῶν καὶ διαφερόντων τῷ ἀριθμῷ κατηγορούμενα, καὶ μήποτε καθοτιοῦν ἑνὶ προσώπῳ περιοριζόμενα. ⟦q16.11|4⟧ Ἐνυπόστατόν ἐστι, τὸ κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν κοινὸν, ἤγουν τὸ εἶδος, τὸ ἐν τοῖς ὑπ᾿ αὐτὸ ἀτόμοις πραγματικῶς ὑφιστάμενον, καὶ οὐκ ἐπινοίᾳ ψιλῇ θεωρούμενον. [bid:c149c]Ἄλλως, ἢ πάλιν ἐνυπόστατόν ἐστι, τὸ ἄλλῳ διαφόρῳ κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν εἰς ἑνὸς σύστασιν προσώπου καὶ μιᾶς γένεσιν ὑποστάσεως, συγκείμενόν τε καὶ συνυφιστάμενον, καὶ οὐδαμῶς καθ᾿ αὐτὸ γνωριζόμενον. ⟦q16.11|5⟧ Ὁμοούσιόν ἐστι τὸ τῆς αὐτῆς οὐσίας ἄλλῳ τυγχάνον, διάφορον δὲ πρὸς τὸ αὐτὸ κατὰ τὴν ὑπόστασιν ὅν· ὡς ἐπί τε ἀνθρώπου καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἔχει εἰδῶν. ⟦q16.11|6⟧ Εἴ τι οὖν ἄλλῳ ταυτὸν ὑπάρχει κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν, οὗ ταυτὸν ὑπάρχει τῷ αὐτῷ καὶ κατὰ τὴν ὑπόστασιν· καὶ εἴ τι ἓν καὶ ἡνωμένον ἄλλῳ τυγχάνει κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν, οὐχ ἓν οὔτε ἡνωμένον τῷ αὐτῷ τυγχάνει καὶ κατὰ τὴν ὑπόστασιν· καὶ εἴ τι διαφορὰν ἔχει πρὸς [bid:c149d]ἄλλο κατὰ τὴν ὑπόστασιν, τοῦτο ἕνωσιν ἔχει πρὸς τὸ αὐτὸ κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν. ⟦q16.11|7⟧ Οὐσιώδης οὖν ἕνωσίς ἐστιν, ἡ τὰς διαφόρους κατ᾿ ἀριθμὸν καὶ πολλὰς ὑποστάσεις εἰς μίαν καὶ τὴν αὐτὴν οὐσίαν συνάγουσα. ⟦q16.11|8⟧ Οὐσιώδης δὲ διαφορὰ τυγχάνει, λόγος καθ᾿ ὃν ἡ οὐσία, ἤγουν φύσις, ἀμείωτός τε καὶ ἄτρεπτος, ἄφυρτος ὁμοῦ καὶ ἀσύγχυτος διαμένει, καὶ τὴν πρὸς ἄλλο κατ᾿ εἶδος ἕτερον εἰς μίαν ὑπόστασιν ποιουμένη σύνοδον, οὐδ᾿ ὅλως τῆς κατὰ φύσιν ἰδίας ἐξίσταται φύσεως. [0152] [bid:c152a]Ὑπόστασις καὶ πρόσωπον, ταυτόν· ἄμφω γὰρ μερικόν τε καὶ ἴδιον, ὡς ἐφ᾿ ἑαυτῶν τὴν περιγραφὴν, ἀλλ᾿ οὐκ ἐν πλείοσι τὴν κατηγορίαν φυσικῶς κεκτημένα. ⟦q16.11|9⟧ Ἐνούσιόν ἐστι τὸ μὴ μόνον ἐνθεωρούμενον ἔχον ἐφ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ τὸ τῶν ἰδιωμάτων ἄθροισμα, καθ᾿ ὃ ἄλλο ἀπ᾿ ἄλλου γνωρίζεται, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ κοινὸν τῆς οὐσίας πραγματικῶς κεκτημένον [n: Sic anima et corpus, quæ partiales substantiæ, non ἐνούσια.]. ⟦q16.11|10⟧ Ὁμοῧπόστατόν ἐστι, τὸ εἰς μίαν καὶ τὴν αὐτὴν ὑπόστασιν ἄλλῳ συντεθειμένον· διάφορον δὲ πρὸς τὸ αὐτὸ κατ᾿ οὐσίαν τυγχάνον· ὡς ἐπί τε ψυχῆς καὶ σώματος ἔχει, καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ὅσα φύσεως ἑτερότητι διαφέροντα, καθ᾿ ὑπόστασιν ἥνωται. ⟦q16.11|11⟧ Εἴ τι οὖν ἄλλῳ καθ᾿ ἕνωσιν συντεθὲν, ταυτὸν ὑπάρχει κατὰ τὴν ὑπόστασιν, τουτέστιν, ὑπόστασις μετ᾿ αὐτοῦ γέγονε [bid:c152b]μία, ἕτερον τῷ αὐτῷ κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν ἐστί. ⟦q16.11|12⟧ Καὶ εἴ τι ἓν καὶ ἡνωμένον ἄλλῳ τυγχάνει κατὰ τὴν ὑπόστασιν, τοῦτο οὐχ ἓν οὔτε ὁμόγενές ἐστι τῷ αὐτῷ καὶ κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν. ⟦q16.11|13⟧ Καὶ εἴ τι συντεθειμένον ἄλλῳ διαφορὰν ἔχει κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν, τοῦτο ἕνωσιν ἔχει πρὸς τὸ αὐτὸ κατὰ τὴν ὑπόστασιν. ⟦q16.11|14⟧ Ὑποστατικὴ οὖν ἕνωσίς ἐστιν, ἡ τὰς διαφόρους οὐσίας ἤγουν φύσεις εἰς ἓν πρόσωπον, καὶ μίαν καὶ τὴν αὐτὴν φυσικὰ θελήματα, μία φύσις, ἢ ἓν φυσικὸν θέλημα γενέσθαι ἄνευ συγχύσεως ἀδύνατον. ⟦q29.1|28⟧ Ἀλλ᾿ ὑποστατικόν; καὶ πάλιν ἀλλοτριώσεις τὸν Υἱὸν τοῦ Πατρὸς, καὶ τρεῖς θελήσεις εἰσάγων φανήσῃ μὴ συμβαινούσας ἀλλήλαις, ὥσπερ καὶ τὰς ὑποστάσεις. ⟦q29.1|29⟧ Ἐὰν εἴπῃς τὴν ὡς ἑνὸς μίαν θέλησιν καὶ ἐνέργειαν [bid:c269b]ἀναγκασθήσῃ τὴν ὡς ἑνὸς τοῦ Πατρὸς, καὶ τὴν ὡς ἑνὸς τοῦ Πνεύματος εἰπεῖν, κἂν θέλῃς καὶ μὴ θέλῃς θέλησιν καὶ ἐνέργειαν, καὶ εὑρεθήσεται εἰς πολυθείαν ἐκπίπτων ὁ λόγος. ⟦q29.1|30⟧ Ἐὰν καὶ σχετικὴν εἴπῃς· Νεστορίου εἰσάγεις προσωπικὴν διαίρεσιν. ⟦q29.1|31⟧ Εἰ δὲ καὶ παρὰ φύσιν εἴπῃς, φθείρεις τὴν ὕπαρξιν τοῦ θέλοντος· φθορὰ γὰρ τῇ φύσει τὸ παρὰ φύσιν ἐστὶ, καθὼς οἱ Πατέρες ὡρίσαντο. ⟦q29.1|32⟧ Ἀλλ᾿ ἄρα τὴν μονάδα πάλιν ἀνασπαράξεις, καὶ εἰς ψήφους ἡμᾶς κινήσεις εἰς διμοιρότριτα τοῦ παρὰ σοῦ ἑνὸς θελήματος, ὅπως μαθεῖν εὕρωμεν κατὰ πόσον ἐστὶ θεῖον, καὶ κατὰ πόσον ἀνθρώπινον. ⟦q29.1|33⟧ Ὁμοίως καὶ κατὰ πόσον ἄκτιστον, καὶ κατὰ πόσον κτιστὸν, καὶ ἀπλῶς ὡς ἔστι σοι φίλον εἰπεῖν. ⟦q29.1|34⟧ Εἰπὲ ἡμῖν τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ θελήματος, τοῦ παρὰ σοῦ πρεσβευομένου ἐπὶ Χριστοῦ. ⟦q29.1|35⟧ Εἰ δὲ καὶ ἀνώνυμον ὑπάρχει κατὰ σὲ τὸ θέλημα τὸ ἓν ὃ λέγεις ἐπὶ Χριστοῦ, σύνταξον αὐτὸ μετὰ τῶν ἀνωνύμων Ψαλμῶν, ὅπως κἂν ἐκεῖ χώραν [bid:c269c]καὶ τόπον εὕρῃ. ⟦q29.1|36⟧ Ἐπειδὴ, λογιώτατε, ἡμεῖς ἀνώνυμον τί ποτε ὁμολογῆσαι οὐ δυνάμεθα. ⟦q29.1|37⟧ Ὡς εἰκὸς δὲ, μέχρι τοῦ νῦν τινὶ τῶν γηγενῶν οὐ πεφανέρωται. ⟦q29.1|38⟧ Ἐγχάραξον οὖν ὁριστικῶς ἐκ πατρικῶν διδασκαλιῶν, καὶ τὴν τοῦ ὀνόματος δήλωσιν διατύπωσον ἡμῖν. ⟦q29.1|39⟧ Ἃ γὰρ ἀριθμοῦμεν [n: Sanctæ scilicet Trinitatis personas.] ἡμεῖς, ταῦτα καὶ ὁμολογοῦμεν, κατὰ τὸν μέγαν καὶ θεοφάντορα Βασίλειον. ⟦q29.1|40⟧ Ἐγὼ λέγω, ὅτι ἡ ζωοποιὸς σὰρξ τοῦ Υἱοῦ τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἐν αὐτῷ ἔσχε τῷ Θεῷ Λόγῳ πάντα τὰ παρφυᾷ τῆς ἰδίας φύσεως, εἰς ἓν πρόσωπον καὶ μίαν ὑπόστασιν τοῦ Θεοῦ Λόγου, τὰς δύο φύσεις συντελούσας. ⟦q29.1|41⟧ Ἕνα γὰρ Υἱὸν, ὡς ἕνα τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος συμπροσκυνοῦμεν Πατρὶ καὶ ἁγίῳ Πνεύματι, ὡς πρὸ τῶν αἰώνων, νῦν καὶ εἰς τοὺς σύμπαντας αἰῶνας, καὶ μετὰ τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ἀμήν.

⟦q29.2|1⟧ ΤΟΥ ΑΥΤΟΥ Κεφάλαια ιʹ περὶ τῶν [n: Turr. γνῶμαι ἀποδεικτικαὶ τῶν.] δύο θελημάτων τοῦ Κυρίου καὶ Θεοῦ καὶ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ. ⟦q29.2|2⟧ Ἐγράφη δὲ πρὸς ὀρθοδόξους.

⟦q29.3|1⟧ αʹ. ⟦q29.3|2⟧ Εἰ ὥσπερ μιᾶς ὑποστάσεως ἐστιν ὁ Λόγος μετὰ [0272] [bid:c272a]τῆς σαρκὸς, οὕτω καὶ ἓν θέλημα κατά τινας, εὐλογημένοι, ἀνάγκη ὥσπερ τῇ ὑποστάσει, οὕτω καὶ τῷ θελήματι καὶ ἡμῶν καὶ τοῦ Πατρὸς διαφέρειν. ⟦q29.3|3⟧ Καὶ πῶς ἡ τῆς φύσεως πρὸς τὸν Πατέρα ταυτότης, τῇ διαφορᾷ τῶν θελημάτων δειχθήσεται;

⟦q29.4|1⟧ βʹ. ⟦q29.4|2⟧ Οἷς ὁ Λόγος τὸ ἓν ἔχει μετὰ τῆς σαρκὸς, τοὺτοις τοῦ Πατρὸς χωρίζεται, καὶ οἷς τὸ ἓν ἔχει μετὰ τοῦ Πατρὸς, τούτοις τῆς σαρκὸς διακρίνεται. ⟦q29.4|3⟧ Εἰ δὲ ἓν θέλημα μετὰ τῆς σαρκὸς κατά τινας, εὐλογημένοι, ἄρα τῷ θελήματι τοῦ Πατρὸς ἐχωρίσθη.

⟦q29.5|1⟧ γʹ. ⟦q29.5|2⟧ Εἰ οἷς ἥνωται ὁ Λόγος τῷ Πατρὶ καὶ τῷ Πνεύματι, τούτοις τῆς σαρκὸς διαφέρειν κρίνεται· ἥνωται δὲ κατὰ τὴν κοινὴν τῶν Χριστιανῶν δόξαν τῷ θελήματι Πατρὶ καὶ Πνεύματι, ἄρα θελήματι τῆς [bid:c272b]σαρκὸς διαφέρει τοῦ Πατρὸς καὶ Πνεύματος, ὡς αὐτοὶ ἑαυτοῖς οἱ Πατέρες καὶ ἡμῖν διωρίσαντο, καὶ ἡμεῖς, εὐλογημένοι, φυλάσσειν σπουδάζομεν.

⟦q29.6|1⟧ δʹ. ⟦q29.6|2⟧ Τοῦτο τὸ ἓν θέλημα, ἢ φυσικὸν ἢ ὑποστατικὸν ἀνάγκη αὐτοὺς, εὐλογημένοι, λέγειν· εἴπερ ἡ τῶν ὄντων σύστασις ἐν οὐσίᾳ καὶ ὑποστάσει θεωρεῖται. ⟦q29.6|3⟧ Τί γὰρ ἂν καὶ εἴη παρὰ ταῦτα ἕτερον λέγειν, [οἷς οὐκ ἐξῆν]; ⟦q29.6|4⟧ Ἀλλ᾿ εἰ μὲν φυσικὸν αὐτὸ εἴπωσι, καὶ μίαν φύσιν λέξουσιν τοῦ Λόγου καὶ τῆς σαρκὸς, καὶ μὴ θέλοντες. ⟦q29.6|5⟧ Εἰ δὲ ὑποστατικὸν, ἀναγκασθήσονται διὰ τὰς ἁγίας τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις, τρία λέγειν καὶ τὰ θελήματα, εἴπερ ἑαυτοῖς στοιχεῖν διέγνωσαν.

⟦q29.7|1⟧ [bid:c272c]εʹ. ⟦q29.7|2⟧ Εἰ τὸ τῆς φύσεως τοῦ Λόγου θέλημα, δημιουργικὸν πάντων τῶν γεγονότων· τοῦτο δὲ κατ᾿ αὐτοὺς, εὐλογημένοι, καὶ τῆς σαρκὸς τυγχάνει θέλημα, δημιουργὸς ἔσται προδήλως τῶν γεγονότων καὶ ἡ τοῦ Λόγου σάρξ. ⟦q29.7|3⟧ Καὶ ἀνῄρηται οὕτω γε ἡ κοινὴ δόξα τῶν Χριστιανῶν, τὸ κτιστὴν αὐτὴν εἶναι. ⟦q29.7|4⟧ Πῶς γὰρ κτίσμα τὸ ἐκ μὴ ὄντων κτίζον, καὶ τὸ ἐξαίρετον τῆς θείας φύσεως ἰδίωμα ἔχον;

⟦q29.8|1⟧ ϛʹ. ⟦q29.8|2⟧ Εἰ διὰ τὸ ἓν θέλημα Πατρὸς καὶ Υἱοῦ καὶ ἁγίου Πνεύματος, καὶ μία φύσις αὐτῶν ἐδείχθη ὑπὸ τῶν θεολήπτων Πατέρων· ἓν δὲ θέλημα κατ᾿ αὐτοὺς, εὐλογημένοι, τοῦ Λόγου καὶ τῆς σαρκὸς, καὶ μία φύσις ἔσται γε οὕτω καὶ τοῦ Λόγου καὶ τῆς σαρκός. ⟦q29.8|3⟧ Εἰ δὲ ἐπὶ τῆς σαρκὸς καὶ τοῦ Λόγου, τὸ ἓν θέλημα [bid:c272d]τὴν μίαν φύσιν οὐ συνάγει, οὐδὲ ἐπὶ Πατρὸς καὶ Υἱοῦ καὶ ἁγίου Πνεύματος, τὸ ἓν θέλημα τὴν μίαν φύσιν συνάξει, καὶ κενὴ ἡ πίστις ἡμῶν, κενὸν τὸ τῶν Πατέρων κήρυγμα.

⟦q29.9|1⟧ ζʹ. ⟦q29.9|2⟧ Τοῦτο τὸ ἓν θέλημα, ἢ προαιρετικὸν τυγχάνει, ἢ φυσικόν. ⟦q29.9|3⟧ Ἀλλ᾿ εἰ μὲν φυσικὸν, καὶ μία φύσις ἔσται, ὡς καὶ ἤδη ἐδείχθη, τῆς σαρκὸς καὶ τοῦ Λόγου· [0273] [bid:c273a]εἰ δὲ προαιρετικὸν, ὥσπερ τῇ ὑποστάσει, οὕτω καὶ τῇ γνώμῃ χωρισθήσεται Πατρὸς καὶ Πνεύματος ὁ Χριστός.

⟦q29.10|1⟧ ηʹ. ⟦q29.10|2⟧ Εἰ κατὰ τὸν μέγαν Κύριλλον, τὰ τῆς αὐτῆς ὄντα οὐσίας καὶ φύσεως, καὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ τυγχάνουσι θελήματος, πῶς τὰ τῆς αὐτῆς μὴ ὄντα φύσεως, τοῦ αὐτοῦ εἶναι θελήματος δύνανται;

⟦q29.11|1⟧ θʹ. ⟦q29.11|2⟧ Εἰ τὸ μὴ θέλειν ἀποθανεῖν, κατὰ τὸ χρυσοῦν στόμα Ἰωάννου, φυσικὸν ἔχει ἡ σάρξ· μετὰ πάντων δὲ τῶν φυσικῶς προσόντων αὐτῇ ἰδιωμάτων ὁ Λόγος ἥνωσεν αὐτὴν ἑαυτῷ ἀτρέπτως καθ᾿ ὑπόστασιν, πῶς τὰ φυσικῶς προσόντα αὐτῇ ἀρνούμενοι, οὐχὶ καὶ τὴν φύσιν τοῖς φυσικοῖς ἰδιώμασι συναρνοῦνται;

⟦q29.12|1⟧ ιʹ. ⟦q29.12|2⟧ Εἰ τῷ θελήματι καὶ πρόσωπον συνεισάγεσθαι [bid:c273b]λέγουσι, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο τὸν οὐκ ὄντα φοβούμενοι φόβον, δύο θελήματα ἐπὶ Χριστοῦ λέγειν οὐκ ἀνέχονται, ἵνα μὴ καὶ δύο πρόσωπα ἐξ ἀνάγκης αὐτοῖς συνεισαχθῇ, βιασθήσονται, εἴπερ εὐσυνάρτητον τὸν τοῦ οἰκείου δόγματος λόγον δεῖξαι βούλονται, ἢ διὰ τὸ ἓν θέλημα τῆς Θεότητος, καὶ ἓν λέγειν πρόσωπον· ἐπειδὴ τῷ θελήματι κατ᾿ αὐτοὺς ἐξ ἀνάγκης καὶ πρόσωπον ἕπεται· ἢ διὰ τὰ τρία πρόσωπα, καὶ τρία θελήματα, Σαβελλίου τε τὴν συναίρεσιν καὶ Ἀρείου τὴν διαίρεσιν εἰσάγειν. ⟦q29.12|3⟧ Ἐπειδὴ δὲ, εὐλογημένοι, ἡ ὁμωνυμία αἴτιον πολλάκις πλάνης γίνεται, τοῦ ἀκροατοῦ πρὸς ἑτέραν σημασίαν μεταβαίνοντος, παρ᾿ ἣν ὑπέφηνεν ὁ λόγος, [bid:c273c]παρακαλῶ τὴν ὑμετέραν ἐν Χριστῷ σύνεσιν, διὰ τὴν[ εὐκρινῆ καὶ ἀσύγχυτον τῶν σημαινομένων πραγμά-] των δήλωσιν, σαφηνίσαι ὑμῖν πρὸ πάντων, εἰ ὅλως ἐστὶ θέλημα, καὶ ἐπὶ ποίων σημαινομένων ἤγουν πραγμάτων φέρεται τὸ τοιοῦτον ὄνομα· καὶ εἰ τὰ μὲν τῶν ὑπ᾿ αὐτὸ προσαγορευομένων πραγμάτων [n: Ita in Basilio, Gregorioque Theologo de Spiritu Deo: in Athanasio περὶ προσώπων in theologia.], σύνθετά εἰσι, τὰ δὲ ἁπλᾶ· καὶ ποῖα δὲ τὰ σύνθετα. ⟦q29.12|4⟧ Καὶ εἰ ἄρα τὰ σύνθετα, ὁμόχρονα ἔχουσι τὰ μέρη, ἢ οὐχ ὁμόχρονα· καὶ ποῖα ποίων προγενέστερα· ποῖα δὲ ποίων μεταγενέστερα. ⟦q29.12|5⟧ Καὶ τίς ὁ ἀποδεικτικὸς ἑκάστου μέρους καὶ ὁριστικὸς λόγος, ἵνα ἔχωμεν νοούμενον, τὸ ἓν θέλημα δέχεσθαι. ⟦q29.12|6⟧ Οὐ γὰρ περὶ φωνῶν ὁ λόγος τοῖς Πατράσιν, ἀλλὰ περὶ πραγμάτων. ⟦q29.12|7⟧ Ὅθεν φωνὰς μὲν παραχωροῦντας τούς. ⟦q29.12|8⟧ Πατέρας εὕρομεν· ἐννοίας δὲ, οὐδαμῶς. ⟦q29.12|9⟧ Πρὸς ἐπὶ] [bid:c273d]τούτοις δὲ, τί προαίρεσις, καὶ τί γνώμη· τί δὸ γνωμικὸν θέλημα, καὶ τί προαιρετικόν; ⟦q29.12|10⟧ Ταῦτα γὰρ πάντα συνδραμεῖν θέλουσι πρὸς τὴν τῶν θελημάτων παράστασιν. ⟦q29.12|11⟧ Καὶ ὁ μὴ ταῦτα γινώσκων μετὰ ἀκριβείας, καὶ περὶ θελημάτων διηγούμενος, τυφλὸς μυωπάζων, μὴ γινώσκων μήτε τί λαλεῖ, μήτε περὶ τίνος διαβεβαιοῦται.

⟦q29.13|1⟧ [0276] [bid:c276a]ΤΟΥ ΑΥΤΟΥ Ἐκ τῶν ἐρωτηθέντων αὐτῷ παρὰ Θεοδώρου μοναχοῦ [n: Videtur hic ipse presbyter Rhaithu, ad quem Περὶ οὐσίας καὶ φύσεως: nec forte alius ad quem Περ⟨…⟩ τῶν δύο θελημάτων.] Φύσις ἐστὶ, κατὰ μὲν φιλοσόφους, ἀρχὴ κινήσεως καὶ ἠρεμίας· κατὰ δὲ τοὺς Πατέρας, εἶδος κατὰ πολλῶν καὶ διαφερόντων τῷ ἀριθμῷ, ἐν τῷ ὁποῖόν τί ἐστι, κατηγορούμενον. ⟦q29.13|2⟧ Οὐσία ἐστὶ, κατὰ μὲν φιλοσόφους, αὐθυπόστατον πρᾶγμα μὴ δεόμενον ἑτέρου πρὸς σύστασιν· κατὰ δὲ τοὺς Πατέρας, ἡ κατὰ πολλῶν καὶ διαφερόντων ταῖς ὑποστάσεσιν ὀντότης καῖ φυσική. ⟦q29.13|3⟧ Ἄτομόν ἐστιν, κατὰ μὲν φιλοσόφους ἰδιωμάτων συναγωγὴ, ὧν τὸ ἄθροισμα ἐπ᾿ ἄλλου θεωρεῖσθαι οὐ δύναται· κατὰ δὲ τοὺς Πατέρας, οἷον Πέτρος [bid:c276b]ἢ Παῦλος, ἤ τις ἕτερος τῶν καθ᾿ αὐτὰ ἰδίοις προσωπικοῖς ἰδιώμασι τῶν ἄλλων ἀνθρώπων ἀφοριζόμενος. ⟦q29.13|4⟧ Ὑπόστασις δέ ἐστιν, κατὰ μὲν φιλοσόφους, οὐσία μετὰ ἰδιωμάτων· κατὰ δὲ τοὺς Πατέρας, ὁ καθ᾿ ἕκαστον ἄνθρωπος, προσωπικῶς τῶν ἄλλων ἀνθρώπων ἀφοριζόμενος.

⟦q29.14|1⟧ Τοῦ ἁγίου Εἰρηναίου ἐπισκόπου Λουγδούνων, μαθητοῦ τοῦ ἁγίου Ἰωάννου τοῦ ἀποστόλου καὶ εὐαγγελιστοῦ [n: Potius Polycarpi et aliorum virorum apostolicorum.], ἐκ τῶν πρὸς Δημήτριον διάκονον Βιαίνης περὶ πίστεως λόγων· οὗ ἀρχὴ, «Ζητῶν τὸν Θεὸν, ἄκουε τοῦ Δαυὶδ λέγοντος.» ⟦q29.14|2⟧ Θέλησις καὶ ἐνέργεια Θεοῦ ἐστιν, ἡ παντὸς χρόνου καὶ τόπου καὶ αἰῶνος, καὶ πάσης φύσεως ποιοτική τε καὶ προνοητικὴ αἰτία. ⟦q29.14|3⟧ Θέλησίς ἐστι τῆς [bid:c276c]νοερᾶς ψυχῆς, ὁ ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν λόγος, ὡς αὐτεξούσιος αὐτῆς ὑπάρχουσα δύναμις. ⟦q29.14|4⟧ Θέλησίς ἐστι νοῦς ὀρεκτικὸς καὶ διανοητικὴ ὄρεξις πρὸς τὸ θεληθὲν ἐπινεύουσα. ⟦q29.14|5⟧ Κλήμεντος τοῦ Στρωματέως, ἐκ τοῦ Περὶ Προνοίας λόγου. ⟦q29.14|6⟧ Θέλησίς ἐστι φυσικὴ δύναμις, τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν ὄντος ὀρεκτική. ⟦q29.14|7⟧ Θέλησίς ἐστι φυσικὴ ὄρεξις, τῇ τοῦ λογικοῦ φύσει κατάλληλος. ⟦q29.14|8⟧ Θέλησίς ἐστι φυσικὴ, αὐτοκράτορος νοῦ αὐτεξούσιος κίνησις· ἢ νοῦς περὶ τι αὐθαιρέτως κινούμενος. ⟦q29.14|9⟧ Αὐτεξουσιότης ἐστὶ νοῦς κατὰ φύσιν κινούμενος· ἢ νοερὰ τῆς ψυχῆς κίνησις αὐτοκρατής.

⟦q29.15|1⟧ [0277] [bid:c277a]Τοῦ ἁγίου Ἀλεξάνδρου πάπα Ἀλεξανδρείας, ἐκ τῆς πρὸς Αἴγλωνα ἐπίσκοπον Κυνοπόλεως [n: Meminerunt Strabo et Ptolemæus. Ægypti olim urbs.] κατὰ Ἀρειανῶν Ἐπιστολῆς. ⟦q29.15|2⟧ Θέλησίς ἐστι φυσικὴ, παντὸς νοεροῦ αὐθαίρετος δύναμις, ὡς μηδὲν κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν ἀκούσιον ἔχοντος.

⟦q29.16|1⟧ Τοῦ ἁγίου Εὐσταθίου Πατριάρχου Ἀντιοχείας, ἐκ τοῦ Περὶ ψυχῆς λόγου. ⟦q29.16|2⟧ Θέλησίς ἐστι φυσικὴ λόγου τοῦ ἐν ἡμῖν κίνησις. ⟦q29.16|3⟧ Θέλησίς ἐστιν ὄρεξις λογική τε καὶ ζωτική.

⟦q29.17|1⟧ Τοῦ ἁγίου Ἀθανασίου πάπα Ἀλεξανδρείας, ἐκ τοῦ Περὶ πίστεως μείζονος λόγου. ⟦q29.17|2⟧ Θέλησίς ἐστι ψυχῆς νοερᾶς αὐτεξούσιος κίνησις. ⟦q29.17|3⟧ Πρῶτον ἰδίωμα τῆς νοερᾶς ψυχῆς, καὶ τῆς οὐσίας [bid:c277b]αὐτῆς δηλωτικόν ἐστιν ἡ θέλησις. ⟦q29.17|4⟧ Νοῦς Κυρίου οὔπω Κύριος, ἀλλ᾿ ἢ θέλησις, ἢ βούλησις ἢ ἐνέργεια.

⟦q29.18|1⟧ Τοῦ ἁγίου Γρηγορίου ἐπισκόπου Νύσσης, ἐκ τοῦ Κατὰ Ἀπολιναρίου λόγου. ⟦q29.18|2⟧ Θέλησίς ἐστι νοῦς τις, καὶ περί τι διάθεσις. ⟦q29.18|3⟧ Αὐτεξουσιότης ἐστὶν, αὐτοκρατὴς τοῦ θελήματος κίνησις. ⟦q29.18|4⟧ Θέλησίς ἐστι τῆς νοερᾶς ψυχῆς, τὸ κατ᾿ ἐξουσίαν αὐτὴν αἱρεῖσθαι τῶν κατὰ γνώμην, διὰ τῆς προαιρετικῆς θελήσεως. ⟦q29.18|5⟧ Θέλησίς ἐστι πάσης λογικῆς φύσεως, ἡ κατὰ φύσιν αὐτῆς ζωή. ⟦q29.18|6⟧ Ἡ στέρησις τῆς οὕτω ζωῆς, οὐσίας ἐστὶν ἀναίρεσις.

⟦q29.19|1⟧ Τοῦ ἁγίου Διαδόχου ἐπισκόπου Φωτίκης, ἐκ τοῦ ἕκτου κεφαλαίου τῶν Ἀσκητικῶν. ⟦q29.19|2⟧ Αὐτεξουσιότης ἐστὶ, ψυχῆς λογικῆς θέλησις ἀκωλύτως [bid:c277c]γινομένη πρὸς ὅπερ ἂν βούληται.

⟦q1.1|1+2+3+4+5+6⟧ [0009] OPUSCULUM 1 — TO MARINUS

⟦q1.1|1+2+3+4+5+6⟧ *Of our father among the saints Maximus the Confessor, to Marinus the most holy presbyter.*

⟦q1.1|1+2+3+4+5+6⟧ Having set thyself as thine aim to journey toward the all-hymned friendship with God, God-honoured Father, thou runnest the course toward it in good order: by reason circumscribing the nature of beings for the coming-to-be of virtue; and by mind, for the establishment of an unerring union [knowledge], bounding the movement of every age and time; with which the longing for God enters in more warmly, both extending the movement of thee who longest alongside the infinity, and by the incomprehensibility of the one longed for making thine aspiration incomprehensible; whose end is God himself, who becomes for the worthy the fulfilment of longing, as self-subsistent enjoyment of good things; of which reason knows experience alone as its comprehension, inasmuch as it is clearly beyond intellection, a union, as of what falls under no intellectual type in any way whatever.

⟦q1.1|1+2+3+4+5+6⟧ For this reason life has become for thee the person of reason, and reason the nature [0012] of life; which together delineate the new man truly according to Christ, bearing by good imitation the image and the likeness of God who created him; which one must now take to be the truth and the goodness: the one being the end of contemplation, the other of practice; and the one the opponent of falsehood, the other of wickedness.

⟦q1.1|1+2+3+4+5+6⟧ Hence to thy achievement of the virtues was joined the comprehension of the divine doctrines, held together by the abundance of knowledge and by the power of demonstration; according to which, having discerned and thrust aside what was put forward without exactness by some concerning wills — who say that will and wish and counsel and choice and inclination, and authority and opinion and prudence, are the same as one another, differing from one another in names alone; and that there will come to be one will of God and of the saints; and who for this reason affirm and insist that Christ has one elective will — thou wast not content with thyself for the confirmation of what had been well judged, because of the poverty of spirit that has been bred up with thee; [n: Matth. v, 3.] but thou didst deign to take me too, who was brought up in unlearnedness, as one casting his vote with thee for what thou hast well recognized. ⟦q1.1|1+2+3+4+5+6⟧ This I come to do, even if it is rash, conquered by the wage of obedience.

⟦q1.1|1+2+3+4+5+6⟧ Of each of these I shall make the writing in sequence, concise and as it were definitional; not engraving words of my own — for how could I, who am poor in these things? — but gathering together what others have laboured over concerning these, that we may know that these differ from one another in both: I mean in name and in reality.

⟦q1.1|1+2+3+4+5+6⟧ *Of natural will, that is, volition.*

⟦q1.1|7⟧ Natural will, that is, volition, they say is a power appetitive of what is according to nature, and holding together all the idioms essentially present to the nature. ⟦q1.1|8⟧ For the essence, naturally held together by this, has appetite for being and living and being moved according to sense and mind, aspiring to its own natural and full true being. ⟦q1.1|9⟧ For the nature is constituted volitive of itself and of all the things that are naturally apt to make up its constitution, being appetitively attached to the principle of its own being, according to which it both is and has come to be.

⟦q1.1|10⟧ Wherefore [0013] others, defining this natural [will], say that will is a rational and vital appetite; and choice a deliberative appetite for things in our power. ⟦q1.1|11⟧ Volition, then, is not choice; if indeed volition is a certain simple appetite, rational and vital, while choice is a concourse of appetite and counsel and judgement. ⟦q1.1|12⟧ For having appetite, we first deliberate; and having deliberated, we judge; and having judged, we choose, in preference to the worse, what has been shown by the judgement to be better. ⟦q1.1|12⟧ And the one depends only on natural things; the other only on things in our power and able to come about through us. ⟦q1.1|13⟧ Choice, then, is not volition.

⟦q1.1|13⟧ *Of wish.*

⟦q1.1|14⟧ But neither is choice wish. ⟦q1.1|15⟧ For wish is an imaginative appetite for things in our power and not in our power, that is, one formed by the understanding alone. ⟦q1.1|16⟧ And the imaginative appetite belongs only to the power of understanding, without the deliberative reason about things in our power; or [it is] a certain qualified natural volition. ⟦q1.1|17⟧ But choice is a deliberative appetite for things to be done that are in our power.

⟦q1.1|18⟧ The account of the description alone, then, having shown the difference of these, would have sufficed to stop from contentiousness those who are superfluously fond of words, and who plainly contradict — I do not know how to say it in seemly terms — what has been well recognized. ⟦q1.1|19⟧ But since those who are eager to learn long somehow to dwell on what is inquired into through more words, we shall say it in another way too. ⟦q1.1|19⟧ Those who have treated of these things say: Not to all to whom choosing is fitting is wishing also altogether fitting. ⟦q1.1|20⟧ For we say that we wish to be healthy and to be rich and to be made immortal; but we do not say that we choose to be rich and to be healthy and to be made immortal; since wish is both of things possible and of things impossible, while choice is of possible things alone, and of those able to come about through us. ⟦q1.1|21⟧ And again, wish is of the end; choice, of the things toward the end. ⟦q1.1|22⟧ They say, then, that the end is the thing wished, for example health; and toward the end, the thing deliberated, for example the mode of health. ⟦q1.1|23+24⟧ The same proportion, then, that the thing wished has to the thing deliberated, they say [0016] wish has to choice; since we choose only those things which we think can come about through us; but we wish also things that cannot come about through us. ⟦q1.1|25⟧ It has been shown, then, that choice is not wish either; and it will be shown again that it is neither deliberation, that is, counsel.

⟦q1.1|26⟧ *Of counsel, that is, deliberation.*

⟦q1.1|27⟧ Counsel, that is, deliberation, they say is an inquiring appetite that comes about concerning some one of the things to be done that are in our power. ⟦q1.1|28⟧ And the thing chosen is what has been judged out of counsel. ⟦q1.1|29⟧ It is clear from this, then, that deliberation is about things still being inquired into, while choice is about things already judged beforehand. ⟦q1.1|30⟧ And this is clear not only from the definition but also from the etymology. ⟦q1.1|31⟧ For the thing chosen (προαιρετόν) is the one taken (αἱρετόν) before (πρό) another. ⟦q1.1|32⟧ And no one prefers anything without having deliberated; nor does he take without having judged. ⟦q1.1|33⟧ Counsel, that is, deliberation, then, is not choice.

⟦q1.1|34⟧ *Of choice.*

⟦q1.1|35⟧ Choice, they say, is a deliberative appetite for things to be done that are in our power. ⟦q1.1|36⟧ For choice is something mixed and blended of many things, composed of appetite and counsel and judgement. ⟦q1.1|37⟧ For choice is none of these considered by itself: it is neither appetite alone by itself, nor counsel, nor judgement; but blended of these, just as the man in our condition is composite of soul and body. ⟦q1.1|38⟧ Since choice comes about, and the thing chosen, at that moment when that which has been preferred out of counsel, which choice is about, takes appetite to itself. ⟦q1.1|39⟧ Necessarily, then, choice is about these things after the judgement, about which counsel is before the judgement. ⟦q1.1|40⟧ For we choose those things about which we deliberate.

⟦q1.1|41⟧ *About what things we deliberate.*

⟦q1.1|42+43⟧ We deliberate about things in our power and able to come about through us, and having an end not evident. 'In our power', then, has been said, since we deliberate only about things to be done; for these are in our power. ⟦q1.1|44⟧ For [we do] not [deliberate] about self-subsistent wisdom. ⟦q1.1|45⟧ For neither about God, nor about things that come about of necessity and always in the same way, such as the cyclic movement of the times; nor about things that are not always, yet come about always alike, such as the rising and setting of the sun; nor about things that are by nature, yet come about not always alike [0017] but for the most part, such as about the sixty-year-old's going grey, or the twenty-year-old's growing a beard; nor about things that are by nature, but come about now one way, now another, indeterminately, such as about rains and droughts and hail. ⟦q1.1|46⟧ For these reasons, then, 'in our power' has been said. ⟦q1.1|46⟧ And 'able to come about through us', since we deliberate neither about all men [all things human], nor about every matter; nor yet about all the things in our power and coming about through us; but there must be added 'and having an end not evident'. ⟦q1.1|47⟧ For if it be manifest and agreed, we no longer deliberate about it, even if it be in our power and come about through us. ⟦q1.1|48⟧ And it has been shown that counsel is not about the end, but about the things toward the end. ⟦q1.1|49⟧ For we deliberate not about becoming rich, but how and by what means we shall become rich. ⟦q1.1|50⟧ And to speak concisely, we deliberate only about those things the doing of which is equally contingent; and that is equally contingent which we are able [to do], both it and what is opposed to it. ⟦q1.1|51⟧ For if we were not able [to do] both, we would not deliberate about both. ⟦q1.1|52⟧ For about things agreed and manifest, or about things impossible and not contingent, no one deliberates. ⟦q1.1|53⟧ And if we were able [to do] only one of the opposites, this would be agreed, as unambiguous, and the opposite impossible. ⟦q1.1|54⟧ For example, when bread and a stone are set before one, no one deliberates which he will make his food, the one being agreed, the other being clearly impossible. ⟦q1.1|55⟧ These, then, we choose: the things equally contingent, about which we also deliberate.

⟦q1.1|55⟧ *Of inclination.*

⟦q1.1|56⟧ But neither is choice some inclination, even if the many readily think so; but it is of inclination; if indeed they say that inclination is an inward appetite for things in our power, from which choice comes; or a disposition toward things in our power that have been appetitively deliberated. ⟦q1.1|57⟧ For appetite, having been disposed toward the things judged out of counsel, has become inclination; after which, or to speak more properly, out of which, comes choice. ⟦q1.1|58⟧ Inclination, then, holds the ratio of habit to operation with respect to choice.

⟦q1.1|59⟧ *Of authority.*

⟦q1.1|60⟧ But neither is choice authority. ⟦q1.1|61⟧ For choice, as I have often said, is a deliberative appetite for things to be done that are in our power; but authority is lawful lordship over things to be done that are in our power; or unhindered lordship over the use of things in our power; or unenslaved appetite for things in our power. ⟦q1.1|62⟧ Authority and choice, then, are not the same; since we choose according to authority, but we do not exercise authority according to choice; and the one only selects, while the other uses the things in our power and the things that bear on the things in our power, that is, choice and judgement and counsel. ⟦q1.1|63⟧ For according to authority we deliberate, [0020] and judge, and choose, and are impelled, and use the things in our power.

⟦q1.1|64⟧ *Of opinion.*

⟦q1.1|65⟧ But neither is choice some opinion. ⟦q1.1|66⟧ For opinion is twofold, rational and irrational; but choice is changeable. ⟦q1.1|67+68⟧ They say, then, that irrational opinion is a simple and ready knowledge, as when someone puts forward another's opinion, not knowing its cause; for example, saying that the soul is immortal, and not giving a demonstrative cause of its immortality. ⟦q1.1|67+68⟧ And rational opinion they say is knowledge constituted by the termination of the understanding, as when someone, having reasoned something out, also renders its cause scientifically. ⟦q1.1|69⟧ For understanding is that which passes through and operates by intervals, beginning from a premise up to a conclusion. ⟦q1.1|70⟧ For example, someone proposes to show the soul immortal, and says: Since the soul is self-moved; and the self-moved is ever-moving; and the ever-moving is immortal: the soul therefore is immortal. ⟦q1.1|71⟧ Or again: Since the soul is incomposite; and the incomposite is indissoluble; and the indissoluble is immortal: the soul therefore is immortal. ⟦q1.1|72+73+74+75+76⟧ For it is proper to understanding to traverse some road leading to the knowledge of the matter; and it travels from the premises through the syllogisms to the conclusions, and makes rational opinion. ⟦q1.1|72+73+74+75+76⟧ And again, opinion is not only of things in our power, but also of things not in our power; but choice is only of things in our power. ⟦q1.1|72+73+74+75+76⟧ And we call opinion true and false; but choice we do not call true and false, but good and bad. ⟦q1.1|72+73+74+75+76⟧ And opinion is of universals; choice, of particulars; for choice is about things to be done, and these are the particulars. ⟦q1.1|72+73+74+75+76⟧ Through more arguments, as I think, it has become manifest that choice is not opinion. ⟦q1.1|72+73+74+75+76⟧ For if opinion, constituted according to the termination of the understanding, is knowledge, while choice is a deliberative appetite for things to be done that are in our power, choice is not the same as opinion.

⟦q1.1|72+73+74+75+76⟧ *Of prudent thought, that is, prudence.*

⟦q1.1|77⟧ But neither is choice prudent thought, that is, prudence. ⟦q1.1|78⟧ If indeed they say that prudence is a contemplative appetite for rational and cognitive learnings; or

⟦q2.1|1⟧ [0021] a habit opposed to both folly and over-subtlety; and choice, as the account has variously rendered it, a deliberative appetite for things in our power. ⟦q2.1|2⟧ And they say that prudence comes about in this manner: for example, the first movement of the mind they call intellection; and the intellection concerning something they call concept; which, having persisted and stamped the soul toward what is understood, is called pondering; and pondering, having remained in the same and having tested itself, is named prudence; and prudence, having been broadened, makes reasoning, which is named the inward word among those skilled in these matters; which, describing it, they say is the fullest movement of the soul, coming about in the reasoning faculty without any utterance; and from it, they say, the uttered word proceeds.

⟦q2.1|3⟧ And again they say that prudent thought is the knowledge of the thing prudently considered, which arises from prudence in the one capable of prudence; for they speak of prudence, and the object of prudence, and the one capable of prudence, and prudent thought. ⟦q2.1|4⟧ And prudence is the relation; the object of prudence is what is prudently considered; the one capable of prudence is what considers prudently; and prudent thought is the knowledge of the thing prudently considered, which has come about from prudence in the one capable of prudence. ⟦q2.1|5⟧ If, then, this is so, but choice is not so, therefore choice is not prudent thought.

⟦q2.1|5⟧ It has been shown, then, clearly, as I think, that the things put forward are not the same as one another, as those hold who think so. ⟦q2.1|6⟧ But if they should say that they are altogether the same as one another, because appetite, that is, the appetitive power of the nature, is predicated equally of all as a genus, let them say also that all the species are the same as one another, the land animals and the winged and the aquatic, because the living being is predicated equally of all as a more generic genus; and the ordering of the universe will be gone for them, being not a hypostasis of different realities, but only a display of bare names.

⟦q2.1|7⟧ *That in every way the will of the saints toward one another and toward God will not be one after the resurrection, even if what is willed is one for all, as some say.*

⟦q2.1|8⟧ So then choice, having taken to itself impulse and use upon the things in our power, is the limit of our rational movement according to appetite. ⟦q2.1|9⟧ For what is rational by nature, having as natural power the rational appetite, which they also call the volition of the intellectual soul, has appetite and reasons; and having reasoned, it wishes. ⟦q2.1|10⟧ For wish, they say, is not the simply natural [volition], but the qualified, that is, the volition concerning something; and [0024] wishing, it inquires; and inquiring, it considers; and considering, it deliberates; and deliberating, it judges; and judging, it chooses; and choosing, it is impelled; and being impelled, it uses; and using, it ceases from the appetitive movement toward that thing. ⟦q2.1|11⟧ For no one uses without first having been impelled; and no one is impelled without choosing; and no one chooses without having judged; and no one judges without having deliberated; and no one deliberates without having considered; and no one considers without having inquired; and no one inquires without having wished; and no one wishes without having reasoned; and no one reasons without having appetite; and no one has rational appetite without being by nature rational. ⟦q2.1|12⟧ Man, then, being by nature a rational living being, is appetitive, and capable of reasoning, of wishing, of inquiry, of consideration; elective, and capable of impulse and of use.

⟦q2.1|13⟧ If, then, along with the rest man is also by nature an elective living being; and choice is of things in our power and able to come about through us and having an end not evident; and in our power is both the principle of the virtues, which is the law of the powers according to nature in operation, and the mode according to the misuse of those same powers, which makes the passions contrary to nature subsist parasitically: therefore everyone elective by nature is receptive of opposites and judging of them. ⟦q2.1|14⟧ And if judging of opposites, altogether elective too; and if elective, since the movement toward both lies under him, he is not unchangeable by nature. ⟦q2.1|15⟧ So then, since counsel and judgement and choice are of things ambiguous, as being in our power, when the ambiguous things are no more, the self-subsistent truth having been shown manifest to all, there is no choice moving through the things that are intermediate and in our power; since there is no judgement either, making the marking-off of opposites, of which we make the better chosen before the worse. ⟦q2.1|15⟧ And if then, according to the law of nature now prevailing, there is no choice, all ambiguity of beings having passed away, there will be only an intellectual appetite in act for those who are thus appetitive according to nature, laying hold ineffably of the mystical enjoyment alone of what is by nature the object of appetite, toward which it had its movement through the things enumerated; whose satiety is the infinite intensification of the very appetite of those who enjoy; each partaking supernaturally as much as he longed; and toward the very thing by nature longed for there is an unmediated co-mingling. ⟦q2.1|16+17+18+19+20⟧ And if as much as each has longed, so much [0025] will he partake of what is longed for, by the principle of nature the volition of all will be shown to be one, but by the mode of movement, different.

⟦q2.1|16+17+18+19+20⟧ And if by the mode according to movement the volition of all men is not one, never will there come to be in every way one volition of God and of those being saved, as it seemed to some; even if what is willed is one for God and for the saints, the salvation of those being saved, which is the divine aim, as the end foreconceived before all the ages; about which there will come about an agreement in volition of those being saved with one another and with God who saves; God having passed wholly into all generically and into each one specifically, he who fills all things by the measure of grace, and is filled in all, like members, according to the proportion of the faith in each, those who have grown together with him. [n: Ephes. i, 23.] For if the will of God is by nature saving, and that of men by nature saved, what saves by nature and what is saved by nature would never be the same; even if the one aim of both is the salvation of all, put forward by God, chosen by the saints.

⟦q2.1|16+17+18+19+20⟧ And if the divine and the human will are to be the same and one in number, according to those who say so, since God made all the ages subsist by will, the choir of the saints will also be creator by the same will, whether natural or of inclination; and, in short, by that by which they are naturally apt to be identified with the divine; which is absurd, and the work, as I think, only of a wandering understanding. ⟦q2.1|16+17+18+19+20⟧ For as long as not all are creators, or only apostles, or only prophets; and these again either Peter only or Moses only; and there are not one but many abodes with the God and Father for the saints; [n: Joan. xiv, 2.] and the human [will], moved by imitation toward the will good by nature, is not the same with it in natural quality and quantity — which is impossible (for how could what is by nature participable be the same as what by nature participates?) — it is impossible that there be in every way one inclination of God and of the choir of the saints; even if, as I said, what is willed is one for both, the salvation of all; about which is the union of the wills.

⟦q2.1|21⟧ But, as it seems, not knowing what an account of absurdity springs up for them from what they say, they let their own understanding be carried aimlessly where it ought not. ⟦q2.1|22⟧ For if there is no will, however it is understood or said, that is without relation and has not the genus 'relative' predicated of it, it is a quality, but not of those that are by themselves, as being, namely, considered in another. ⟦q2.1|23⟧ And if the will is of those considered in another, it is altogether an accident; and if an accident, it will be characteristic either of essence or of hypostasis (for [0028] there is nothing intermediate between these considered by itself, either partaking of neither, or composite from both). ⟦q2.1|23⟧ And if of essence, they will predicate one nature of God and of the saints, all having undergone, through the one will, coalescence into one essence. ⟦q2.1|24⟧ For what is predicated generically of certain things equally is indicative of the essence under which they fall. ⟦q2.1|25⟧ And if of hypostasis, there will be one hypostasis of all, of God and of the saints, all having been fused into the same with one another. ⟦q2.1|26⟧ For what is specifically innate in someone according to hypostasis, being considered invariantly in others, confounds all with one another, and makes the principle of the how-to-be of each one altogether indiscernible.

⟦q2.1|27⟧ *That it is not possible that one will be said of Christ, whether it be called natural or elective, as it seemed to some.*

⟦q2.1|28⟧ So then, if their account was weak in these matters, neither when it passes to our Lord and God and Saviour of all, Christ, and constructs one will said of him in whatever way, would it ever be strong. ⟦q2.1|29⟧ For if they should say that this will of Christ is natural, they will be shown sick straightaway with the Manichaean fantasy, as maintaining one nature of Christ, which is not and will not be, revealed by a corresponding will; and they will be caught at the same time emulating the madness of Arius and the essence-fusion of Apollinarius, as alienating Christ according to essence from the God and Father and from the immaculate Mother. ⟦q2.1|30⟧ For the natural will characterizes nature; and no account will contradict this. ⟦q2.1|31⟧ And if it characterizes nature, it is clear that those who say this proclaim Christ a nature. ⟦q2.1|32⟧ And if Christ is a nature, he is neither God by nature nor yet truly man by nature; if indeed the Father is not truly Christ by nature, nor the Mother truly Christ by nature. ⟦q2.1|33⟧ And if Christ is God by nature inasmuch as he is by nature Christ, he who says this is a polytheist, maintaining one nature of the Father as God, who is not by nature Christ, and another nature of Christ as God, who is by nature Christ; and the end of such portent-mongering for them will be condemnation for polytheism.

⟦q2.1|34⟧ And if [they call it] elective, which they call [will] of inclination, it will either be altogether according to nature, having the mode of the use of the things to be done that lie with Christ converging in all things with the principle of nature; and thus Christ will be shown, according to them, not impassible but self-mastering of passions; and good by progress, whatever he is in nature. ⟦q2.1|35⟧ For such is choice according to nature of the things to be done that lie with the one choosing, making the better chosen before the worse; or

⟦q3.1|1⟧ [0029] contrary to nature, and it will show the mode of the use of the things that lie with him as having become destructive of the principle of nature; for such is choice contrary to nature of the things to be done that lie with the one choosing, making the worse chosen before the better. ⟦q3.1|2⟧ For when the judgement of the one choosing, according to deliberation, about the things to be done that lie with him has been set right or has slipped — of which judgement choice is, as it were, the vote — either the principle according to nature subsists for him through good use, or the mode contrary to nature subsists parasitically through bad use: the one becoming the messenger of choice according to nature, the other of choice contrary to nature.

⟦q3.1|2⟧ And if the choice of Christ be according to nature, not only shall we again blame them for the same things, as rashly improvising another nature of Christ, intermediate between Godhead and creation; but we shall also laugh at them as triflers, making Christ, like a mere man according to Nestorius, receptive of opposites by nature according to choice. ⟦q3.1|3⟧ And if contrary to nature, I pass over the blasphemy in silence, lest unawares I defile my tongue with the refutations against them. ⟦q3.1|4⟧ For in saying there is an elective will in Christ, they have altogether indicated that the hypostasis of Christ is able to be moved according to nature and contrary to nature. ⟦q3.1|5⟧ For such, as I said before, is choice; and if it is characteristic of the hypostasis of Christ, they have marked him off, by this very will, from both the Father and the Spirit as of other counsel and of other inclination. ⟦q3.1|6⟧ For what is considered specifically in the Son according to hypostasis is altogether incommunicable to the Father and the Spirit according to hypostasis. ⟦q3.1|7⟧ As many, then, of the holy Fathers as made mention of choice in the manhood of Christ indicated the appetitive power of the nature essentially — which is the same as saying the natural volition — or our own choice, present in God incarnate by appropriation.

⟦q3.1|8⟧ Having considered this especially, I, thy servant and disciple, in what was set out to my most holy lord and teacher Thalassius concerning the difficulties of holy Scripture, said "choice"; knowing that if the maker of men has become man for us, he has clearly also achieved for us the unchangeableness of choice, as creator of unchangeableness; [0032] receiving essentially and by authority the passions of our penalty through the experience itself, while taking upon himself those of dishonour by appropriation, in his love for man; of which he has made the appropriation the cause to the race of the elective dispassion, and has given the experience as a faithful pledge of the natural incorruption that will follow. ⟦q3.1|9⟧ For the human of God was not moved by choice as we are, making the discernment of opposites through counsel and judgement, lest it be thought changeable by nature according to choice; but having received its being together with the union with God the Word, it had its natural movement according to appetite, that is, volition, undoubting, or rather stable; or, to speak more properly, it had its rest unmoved in him, according to the most unalloyed essentiation, altogether deified by God and Word; which rest he, naturally shaping and moving it as his own and natural to his own soul, has fulfilled without fantasy the great mystery of the economy on our behalf; having diminished nothing at all natural of what was assumed, except sin, of which no principle at all has been sown in any of the things that are.

⟦q3.1|10⟧ The difference of the names, then, having become manifest to us through the description distinctly fitted to each, let us not be troubled when we hear those who use the names without distinction for the confusion of the realities understood; since for us the truth is in realities, and not in names; and let us not think what is not the same to be the same; but believing piously, let us confess Christ truly perfect God and truly perfect man, the same being so in reality, properly, in truth, and not called this by bare name alone; and for this reason let us proclaim two natures, of which he is hypostasis, if indeed we do not proclaim him fleshless; and two natural wills, according to the Fathers, if indeed we boldly declare that he is not soulless and mindless; and let us not dare to innovate a word for which we have no refuge in the authority of the Fathers. ⟦q3.1|11⟧ For one will of Christ, natural or elective, those zealous to be pious fear to say, not only because of the absurdity shown, [0033] but because no one of the holy teachers has ever been found to have said it; knowing truly that choice belongs to things able to be moved to both — I mean good things and bad; which in the case of Christ, the very essence and source of good things, even to conceive, not to say to speak of, is fullest of all impiety. ⟦q3.1|12⟧ And concerning these things, so much.

⟦q3.1|13⟧ Concerning the one operation lying in the seventh chapter of the Difficulties of the great Gregory, the account is clear. ⟦q3.1|14⟧ For describing the future state of the saints, I said there was one operation of God and of the saints, the one deifying all the saints, of the hoped-for blessedness: belonging to God by essence, but having come about for the saints by grace. ⟦q3.1|15⟧ Or rather, I added "of God alone"; since the deification of the saints by grace is the effect of the divine operation alone, of which we do not have the power sown in our nature. ⟦q3.1|16⟧ And of what we do not have the power, of these neither do we have the practice, which is the completion of natural power. ⟦q3.1|17⟧ Practice, then, depends on power; and power on essence. ⟦q3.1|18⟧ For practice is from power; and power from the essence and in the essence. ⟦q3.1|19⟧ These three, then, as they say, depend on one another: what is able, power, the possible. ⟦q3.1|20+21+22+23+24⟧ And "what is able" they say is the essence; power, that according to which we have the movement of being able; and the possible, what is naturally apt to come about by us according to power. ⟦q3.1|20+21+22+23+24⟧ And if what is naturally apt to come about by us we have according to natural power; but deification is not of the things naturally apt to come about by us according to power, not being of the things in our power — for there is no principle in nature of things above nature — therefore deification is not the practice of our power, of which we do not have the power according to nature, but of the divine power alone; being not a requital to the saints for just works, but a demonstration of the bounty of the one who made them; who makes the lovers of good things by adoption that which he himself will be shown to be by nature, according to the principles which he himself knows; that he may both be perfectly known, and remain altogether incomprehensible. ⟦q3.1|20+21+22+23+24⟧ I did not, then, destroy the natural operation of those who will undergo this, by making it manifest that it has ceased from what it is naturally apt to accomplish, and undergoes only the enjoyment of good things; but I indicated [0036] that the superessential power alone is productive of deification, having come about by grace for those deified.

⟦q3.1|25⟧ And let no one suspect that by these things one operation of Christ is proclaimed. ⟦q3.1|26⟧ For we do not proclaim Christ a deified man, but God perfectly become man, and having made manifest, through flesh operative by nature, intellectually ensouled, the infinite — infinitely-many times, infinitely more than infinite — power of his own ineffable Godhead; the same wholly God and truly man; the same perfect and most full in both by nature, and having without deficiency all that is naturally in both, except sin, of which there is no principle. ⟦q3.1|27⟧ For of the natures of which he was hypostasis, of these he also naturally received the essential principles. ⟦q3.1|28⟧ And if he received the essential principles of those of which he was hypostasis, he also fittingly had the natural ensouled operation of the flesh, whose essential principle is sown in the nature. ⟦q3.1|29⟧ And if he had as man natural operation, whose principle was constitutive of the nature, he clearly also had as God natural operation, whose principle was manifestive of the superessential Godhead. ⟦q3.1|30⟧ For being perfect God and the same perfect man, he operated naturally according to each of those of which he was hypostasis, not being divided. ⟦q3.1|31⟧ And if he operated naturally according to each of those of which he was hypostasis, not being divided, it is clear that with the natures of which he was hypostasis he also had their essential and constitutive operations, of which he himself was the union; operating congruously with himself, and through the things he operated confirming the truth of those from which, and in which, and which he was.

⟦q3.1|32⟧ One, then, is Christ from two natures, Godhead and manhood; only-begotten Word and Son and Lord of glory; in which he is known, and which he is truly believed to be; having two natural and generic movements, that is, operations, constitutive of those from which he was; whose results were the effects of operation in detail, both put forth from him and perfected by him, without cut of those from which he was, and apart from any confusion whatever. ⟦q3.1|33⟧ For he does not undergo cut or confusion who is never subject to changes, and who provides to all the things that are the permanence and constitution both of being and of how-to-be.

⟦q3.1|33⟧ [0037] These things, by thy command, sanctified Father, let it be said, have been set out in brief; that thou mayest have, if they bring anything useful, the means to beat off the chatter of the talkative, which has taken licence from the difficulty of the times. ⟦q3.1|34⟧ And do not overlook thy servant, who is poor; but enrich him with the divine Spirit, repaying his obedience with thy strong prayers; and do not cease commending [me] to Christ the great God and Maker of all, who is worshipped by all creation, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, unto the ages. ⟦q3.1|35⟧ Amen.

⟦q3.2|1⟧ SCHOLIA

⟦q3.3|1⟧ 1. ⟦q3.3|2⟧ By reason the nature of beings is circumscribed for the coming-to-be of virtue, by way of procession; which is the complete denial of nature according to virtue. ⟦q3.3|3⟧ And by mind the movement of every age and time is bounded, for the establishment of an unerring union, by way of ascent; which is the surpassing of the things in which nature is — I mean place and time, in which is the hypostasis of beings. ⟦q3.3|4⟧ And the restoration by grace toward him from whom are all things, and through whom, and to whom, as the limit of all, comes about by way of taking-up; which is a passion of the one taken up, but an operation of the one taking up.

⟦q3.4|1⟧ 2. ⟦q3.4|2⟧ Person, that is, hypostasis; nature, that is, essence. ⟦q3.4|2⟧ For essence is the "according to the image", reason; and the "according to the likeness", life, is hypostasis; out of both of which virtue has been completed. ⟦q3.4|3⟧ For they say that virtue is the hypostasis of wisdom, and that wisdom is the essence of virtue. ⟦q3.4|4⟧ Wherefore the unerring manifestation of wisdom is the mode of the conduct of the contemplative; and the base of virtue is the principle of the contemplation of the practical. ⟦q3.4|5⟧ And the most unlying character of both is the unswerving gazing toward what properly is.

⟦q3.5|1⟧ 3. ⟦q3.5|2⟧ That man is not unchangeable by nature; and how.

⟦q3.6|1⟧ 4. ⟦q3.6|2⟧ That the will is characteristic either of essence or of hypostasis; and there is nothing intermediate between these, neither common and composite from both, nor partaking of neither.

⟦q3.7|1⟧ 5. ⟦q3.7|2⟧ That choice in the case of Christ signifies the natural volition, that is, the appetitive power of the nature.

⟦q3.7|3⟧ 6. ⟦q3.7|3⟧ See the mystery of the economy.

⟦q3.7|4⟧ 7. ⟦q3.7|4⟧ On "For through him we live and move and are"; that is, concerning essence and power and operation.

⟦q3.8|1⟧ 8. ⟦q3.8|2⟧ On deification. ⟦q3.8|3⟧ Mayest thou too hear these things, Nilus; and mayest thou think what the teachers of the truth think.

⟦q4.1|1⟧ [0040] OPUSCULUM 2 — TO THE SAME MARINUS: FROM THE TREATISE ON OPERATIONS AND WILLS, CHAPTER 50

⟦q4.1|1⟧ *Of the same, to the same Marinus.* ⟦q4.1|2⟧ *From the treatise on operations and wills, chapter 50.*

⟦q4.1|2⟧ *That Severus maliciously says that the hypostasis is the same as the nature, in order that he may ratify the confusion through the one nature, and may escape the refutation by saying that he understood the nature to be hypostasis; and may again introduce the division, advocating the union from hypostases; and may seem to escape notice, asserting that he takes the hypostases in place of natures. ⟦q4.1|3⟧ And again, when accused of the non-existence of the natures through the bare difference, he may find a refuge of defence, the bare difference in natural quality. ⟦q4.1|4⟧ And that, just as Nestorius, saying the union was bare, introduced a real division, so Severus too, saying the difference of natures is bare, makes the confusion real.*

⟦q4.1|5⟧ But Severus, hard pressed by these arguments, and not bearing the testing of the truth, again, as is his custom, puts forward falsehood for himself as an ally: asserting that in the economy the hypostasis is the same as the nature, and the difference in natural quality the same as the real one and that according to nature, on the ground that every quality too is natural, and is called a thing; so that, if, caught by the refutations, he should be detected plainly, through the one composite nature, advocating the phantasy of Manes, and the confusion of Apollinarius, and Eutyches' coalescence of the things united into one essence after the union, he may, after the manner of a chameleon changing its colours, alter his own word, asserting that he understood the nature to be hypostasis. ⟦q4.1|6⟧ But if again, saying that the union came about from hypostases, that is, persons, he should be shown to think the division of Ebion, of Paul of Samosata and of Nestorius, and to decree the operation of the Word by grace, as in a prophet, he may [0041] again have falsehood ready as his advocate, declaring that he said hypostases in place of natures. ⟦q4.1|7⟧ But if again he should be justly accused, upon the bare difference, of dogmatizing the non-existence of the things united, he may find as a refuge for his defence the difference as in natural quality, saying that after the union there is in Christ a difference of natural qualities, but not of natures, that is, of essences: through the word that dissolves the confusion, that is, the difference, the crafty sophist binding the confusion the tighter; making contraries not, according to the law of nature, a dissolution of contraries, but, against the definition and law of nature, their constitution; and becoming, to the deceiving of his hearers, such concerning the difference as Nestorius was shown to be concerning the union. ⟦q4.1|8⟧ For that one, naming the union by the bare appellation alone, introduced in operation the division of the things; and this one, advocating the bare difference after the union, thinks the existence of the things differing to be in conception, but in operation contrives their confusion.

⟦q4.1|9⟧ For if Nestorius had not thought that the union came about bare, he would have said the one composite hypostasis of Christ, completed from the union of the natures; and this one, if he had not proclaimed the difference bare, would not have refused to say, in Christ after the union, the uncut and undivided quantity of the things differing, knowing that with every difference quantity is altogether introduced together, and with every quantity the number indicative of it is yoked. ⟦q4.1|9⟧ For it is impossible either for difference to be without quantity, or for quantity to be discerned apart from the number that indicates it.

⟦q4.1|10⟧ And the one, knowing in Christ only the quantity of the natures, and not knowing the singleness of the hypostasis according to composition from the natures, makes the bare appellation of the union a covering, through and through, of the division of the natures; the other, advocating the singleness according to the nature alone instead of that according to hypostasis, and not knowing the quantity according to nature, makes the bare difference in natural quality a covering of the confusion of the natures. ⟦q4.1|11⟧ And the one, advocating the union of the natures in a quality of inclination alone, denies the one hypostasis, not enduring to say that the concourse of the things according to essence came about true. ⟦q4.1|12⟧ For authority and worth, and a volition of such a kind, of which Nestorius asserted the union to be, are plainly movements of inclination, but not of nature. [0044] But the other, saying the bare difference after the union in natural quality alone, evidently makes an destruction of the things united, denying the difference according to essence, in natural otherness, of the very things united.

⟦q4.1|13⟧ And to speak of these briefly: the one devised the union of the qualities of inclination for the division of the things that are by nature; the other, on the contrary, contrived the difference of the natural qualities for the confusion of the things. ⟦q4.1|14⟧ Truly an evil pair of lawless men, raging evilly to tear apart through contraries the truth of the right doctrines. ⟦q4.1|15⟧ For the one, introducing a union of qualities of inclination, makes a division of the natures which in his view were in no way united; the other, saying that after the union there is only a difference of natural qualities, likewise introduces a confused alteration of the natures which in his view were in no way united; not knowing what they are saying. ⟦q4.1|16⟧ For they ought, if they had resolved to keep in line with themselves: Nestorius, saying that the union came about of qualities of inclination, not to divide the natures, of which he did not in the least advocate a union from the beginning, but to recognize after the union the difference of those of which he asserts the union to be; and Severus, introducing a difference of natural qualities, not to confuse after the union the natures, of which we do not concede to him to speak of the union so long as he is ignorant of their difference after the union. ⟦q4.1|17⟧ For of the things united the difference is contemplated after the union, even if Nestorius rave; and of the things differing after the union there is the union, even if Severus set himself in battle array, and make a great advocacy on behalf of falsehood.
