⟦q17.1|1+2+3+4+5+6⟧ OPUSCULUM 15 — SPIRITUAL AND DOGMATIC TOME AGAINST THE EKTHESIS

⟦q17.1|1+2+3+4+5+6⟧ *Of the holy Maximus. ⟦q17.1|1+2+3+4+5+6⟧ A spiritual and dogmatic tome, showing that the intrusive Ekthesis of Heraclius the emperor, which came about by way of innovation at the suggestion of Sergius, president of Constantinople, is discordant with the sacred Oracles and the Fathers, but concordant with the unholy [0156] heretics who tell monstrous tales of confusion and division alike in the mystery of Christ our God. ⟦q17.1|1+2+3+4+5+6⟧ Written from Rome to Stephen, the most holy bishop of Dora, ranking under the holy and apostolic throne of the holy city of Christ our God.*

⟦q17.1|1+2+3+4+5+6⟧ The Lord, having likened the present life to night, its movement to a mill, and its rest to a bed, determined that of those who are in each (I mean the mill and the bed) the one is taken and the other left. [n: Matth. xxiv, 41; Luc. xvii, 34.] And to be taken is perhaps the one who has been released from the former through contemplation and from the latter through practice, and who has remained, by disposition, neither in the circumscription of the intervals, in which the movement of the things that are seen is seen, nor in the softness of the passions, in which is the rest; but to be left is he who is held fast in these by self-choice, through the soul's love of pleasure and love of the lofty.

⟦q17.1|1+2+3+4+5+6⟧ But what then? ⟦q17.1|1+2+3+4+5+6⟧ Having learned by trial before, as by hearing today, that I your servant am held fast, how could you, O God-illumined and all-excellent ones, have chosen, in what you have written, to be brought down so sympathetically to condescension toward the poor and needy man — you who have been so far lifted from the earth according to the grace of God, and exalted, as to raise up your life to reason, and your mind to the Lord of the things here, and above the things here; appropriating and making one the image to the archetype; or, to say it more truly, wishing to make the self-chosen condescension of your supreme beauty a demonstration of height, so that by its abundance you might lead us also to the measure of the more-than-infinite God the Word, who by his self-emptying toward us showed uncircumscribably the height of his own glory; to the end that he might refashion us the more longingly, by as much as he himself, for our sake, formed himself in flesh toward what is lowlier: become man by nature without change and confusion, he who is surpassingly the lover of man; leaving nothing lacking for the assumption of what is ours, lest he leave both the grace lacking to himself and the salvation lacking to us, not giving it whole to the nature, as not having taken the nature whole, but diminishing it in that respect in which he had not assumed it.

⟦q17.1|1+2+3+4+5+6⟧ «For what is unassumed is unhealed,» says the great Gregory. ⟦q17.1|7⟧ For how would God the Word, the superessential, incarnate for us from the Holy Spirit and Mary the Ever-Virgin and Mother of God by the assumption of flesh having the intellectual and rational soul, having become new and come to be man by nature, renew the ancient [man], had he not taken him wholly and whole, apart from sin alone, from which comes the growing-old, and through which death was decreed against the nature, having us for its food so far as we tasted of that [sin], bitterly glutted with the tree of the transgression? ⟦q17.1|8⟧ And how would the same, emptied, raise up the fallen one, had he not united him to himself wholly and whole according to hypostasis from the very first point of conception, apart from the slip alone, [0157] from which comes the breaking, and on account of which the penalty?

⟦q17.1|9⟧ Thus, then, having assumed the intellectual and rational soul together with the body grown together with it, that is, perfect man, without any blemish, and having united it to himself according to hypostasis, he who is God above nature, having taken also its natural [volition], had in every way a self-determining volition. ⟦q17.1|10⟧ If, transgressing the commandment, we transgressed by volition, and not apart from volition, we needed the healing that concerns it, God incarnate himself healing like by the assumption of like; and having assumed it, he would also have had its rational and vital operation, by which, having reasoned out and operated sin — would that we never had! — we stood in need of the salvation that concerns it, he cleansing it of every defilement by the assumption, and making divine our whole nature by the incarnation.

⟦q17.1|11⟧ For if God the Word created this [nature] having these things essentially — I mean the volition and the operation — and presented the one as self-determining and the other as operating, it is clear that, having taken the nature, he united it to himself according to hypostasis just as he created it from the beginning, that is, volitive by nature and operative; so that it should not be that, had he assumed only the suffering nature but not also its innate powers, he would not even have assumed the nature, but made a phantasm of the economy. ⟦q17.1|12⟧ For it is impossible for ours, or for the nature of any other of the things that are, ever to be or to be named a nature apart from its innate powers, by which each is naturally characterized essentially. ⟦q17.1|13+14⟧ Hence our nature is not without volition, since then it would not even be a man's; nor indeed without operation, since it is not soulless. ⟦q17.1|15⟧ But if he was without volition and without operation as regards what is ours, as seemed to some of the heretics of old and of now, then he who is above us did not at all come to be as we are, not confirming what is ours by what is ours, and by the things by which he himself, having created man from the beginning, characterized him naturally, making him self-determining and operative according to nature.

⟦q17.1|16+17⟧ And indeed the composition of the holy Gospels confirms incontrovertibly that he assumed the power of each of these, by those [passages] in which it presents the superessential Word, become man for us, as willing and operating; crying out in one place: *And about the fourth watch of the night he comes to them walking upon the sea, and he willed to pass by them;* [n: Marc. vi, 48.] in another: *And arising from there into the borders of Tyre and Sidon, and entering into a house, he willed that no one should know, and he could not be hid;* [n: Marc. vii, 24.] and again: *Going out from there they passed through Galilee, and he did not will that anyone should know;* [n: Marc. ix, 29.] and: *On the morrow he willed to go forth into Galilee.* [n: Joan. i, 43.] And after these, again: *Jesus walked in Galilee, for he did not will to walk in Judaea, because the Jews sought to kill him;* [n: Joan. vii, 1.] and: *Where wilt thou that we prepare for thee to eat the passover?* [n: Matth. xxvi, 17.] and: [0160] *They gave him vinegar mingled with gall, and having tasted he did not will to drink.* [n: Matth. xxvii, 34.]

⟦q17.1|18⟧ For these — I mean *He willed to pass by them*, and *He willed to go forth*, and *He did not will to walk*, and *to will to eat the passover*, and *not to will to drink the vinegar* — confirm his human volition and operation, as ours is. ⟦q17.1|19⟧ For example, to will and not to will to pass by, or to eat, or to walk, or to drink, is plainly volition, by which he was known to be volitive by nature. ⟦q17.1|20⟧ But by tasting and eating, and going forth, and journeying from place to place and walking, he was plainly shown, as being operative, [to have] the operation according to which he later became man by nature for our sake, but not according to that which he was without beginning, through himself, by nature, God. ⟦q17.1|21+22⟧ For it is not natural to the Word, in that he was God and Son of God according to nature, to will anything bodily and to eat, or to be confined locally by movements from place to place, being everywhere and above the all, infinitely, infinite times over. ⟦q17.1|21+22⟧ So too [Scripture], presenting him as having superessentially the divine and paternal volition and operation, teaches clearly: *As the Father raises the dead and gives life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills.* [n: Joan. v, 21.] Here, then, too, to will to give life to the dead bears witness to his divine volition; and to give life itself, to his properly all-working operation. ⟦q17.1|23⟧ And simply, whatever else is such depends from the nature exalted above the things that are, for the manifestation of it, so far as possible.

⟦q17.1|24⟧ By these, then, the Word himself, through his own disciples, presents himself, according to both his natures, from which and in which he consists, as being volitive by nature and operative of our salvation; and those after them, their successors and the revealers of the theophany of the Word in the flesh, the God-chosen Fathers of the catholic Church, proclaiming alike each nature of the same, both the divine and the human, and not only that, but also the volition and the operation, say these things with a great voice. ⟦q17.1|25⟧ For the one named for immortality, in his discourse on the incarnation and the Trinity: [n: Matth. xxvi, 39.] «And when he says, *Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless not mine, but thy will be done*; and again, *The spirit indeed is eager, but the flesh weak*, he shows here two wills: the human, on account of the weakness of the flesh, refuses the passion, but his divine [will] is eager.» ⟦q17.1|26⟧ And Gregory, named for Theology, in his second [0161] discourse on the Son: «Let the seventh be said: that the Son has come down from heaven, not that he might do his own will, but that of him who sent him. ⟦q17.1|27+28⟧ If, then, these things were not being said of him who came down, we should say that the word is shaped as about the man — not him who is understood in the Saviour, for his will is not even opposed to God, being wholly deified — but him who is as we are; since the human will does not wholly follow the divine, but for the most part resists and wrestles against it.»

⟦q17.1|29⟧ And his namesake, who became the guide of the Nyssenes, or rather the teacher of the inhabited world, in his discourse on the Pascha: [n: Matth. xv, 32 seqq.] «The leper approaches, already wasted away and made useless in body. ⟦q17.1|30⟧ How does the healing come to him from the Lord? ⟦q17.1|31⟧ The soul wills, the body touches; through both the passion flees. ⟦q17.1|31⟧ *For the leprosy*, he says, *departed from him at once*.» ⟦q17.1|32⟧ And again the same in the same discourse: «Again, those who in many thousands waited on him in the desert he does not will to dismiss fasting; but with his hands he breaks the loaves. ⟦q17.1|33⟧ Seest thou how through both the Godhead, accompanying, is made public — by the body that operates, and by the impulse of the will that arises in the soul?» ⟦q17.1|34⟧ And in the second book of those he laboured against Eunomius the impious: «How did the Lord, reconciling the world to himself, distribute to soul and body the benefaction that came from him to men, willing through the soul, and touching through the body?» ⟦q17.1|35⟧ And again the same says, in his [books] against Apollinarius: [n: Matth. xxvi, 39.] «Since, then, the human will is one thing and the divine another, he who made our passions his own utters, as from the man, what is suited to the weakness of the nature; but he adds the second utterance, willing that the lofty purpose befitting God be ratified above the human for the salvation of the world. ⟦q17.1|36⟧ For he who said *Not mine* signified the human by the word; and adding *But thine*, he showed the conjoinedness of his Godhead with the Father, of which there is no difference of will, on account of the communion of the nature.»

⟦q17.1|37⟧ And the divine John, who made illustrious the throne of the queen [city], in the discourse entitled *Against those who stayed away from the synaxis, and a demonstration that the Son is consubstantial with the Father*, [0164] whose beginning is *Again horse-races, and again our assembly has become smaller*: [n: Joan. x, 30.] «Seest thou how he also proclaimed beforehand his former age? ⟦q17.1|37⟧ Ask the heretic, then: Does God fear and shrink back? ⟦q17.1|38+39⟧ And does he hesitate and grieve? ⟦q17.1|38+39⟧ And if he says Yes, stand off from him henceforth, and set him down below with the devil, or rather lower even than him; for not even he will dare to say this. ⟦q17.1|40⟧ But if he says that none of these things is worthy of God, say: Then neither does God pray. ⟦q17.1|41⟧ For apart from these, another absurdity also follows, if the words are God's. ⟦q17.1|42⟧ For the words show not only agony, but two wills, one of the Son and one of the Father, contrary to each other. ⟦q17.1|43⟧ For to say *Not as I will, but as thou* is [the word] of one who shows this. ⟦q17.1|44⟧ But this not even those [heretics] ever conceded; but when we always say *I and the Father are one* of the power, they say this was said of the volition, saying that the wish of the Father and the Son is one. ⟦q17.1|45⟧ If, then, the wish of the Father and the Son is one, how does he say here: *Nevertheless not as I will, but as thou*? ⟦q17.1|46⟧ For if what is said is said of the Godhead, a contradiction arises, and many absurdities are begotten from it. ⟦q17.1|47⟧ But if of the flesh, what is said has reason, and there would be no charge. ⟦q17.1|48+49⟧ For it is no condemnation that the flesh does not will to die; for this is of nature. ⟦q17.1|50⟧ For he shows all the things of nature without sin, and with much abundance, so as to stop the mouths of the heretics. ⟦q17.1|51⟧ When, then, he says *If it be possible, let this cup pass from me*, and *Not as I will, but as thou*, he shows nothing else than that he truly put on flesh that fears death. ⟦q17.1|52⟧ For to fear death, and to shrink back, and to be in agony, is of that [flesh]. ⟦q17.1|53⟧ Now, then, he leaves it desolate and stripped of its own operation, so that, having shown its weakness, he might confirm its nature as well; and now he hides it, so that thou mayest learn that he was not a bare man. ⟦q17.1|54⟧ For just as, if he had shown human things throughout, he would have been thought this, so if he had accomplished the things of the Godhead throughout, the account of the economy would have been disbelieved. ⟦q17.1|55⟧ For this reason he varies and mixes both the words and the deeds, so that he may give no pretext to the disease and madness either of Paul of Samosata or of Marcion and Manichaeus. ⟦q17.1|56⟧ For this reason he both foretells what is to be as God, and shrinks back again as man.»

⟦q17.1|57⟧ And let us hear clearly what Cyril, the guide of the Alexandrians, teaches in the twenty-fourth chapter of the *Thesaurus*: «When, then, he appears fearing death and saying, *If it be possible, let this cup pass from me*, consider again that the flesh, fearing death, was being taught, borne by God the Word, no longer to suffer this; for he was saying

⟦q18.1|1⟧ [0165] to the Father: *Not as I will, but as thou.* ⟦q18.1|2+3⟧ For he himself did not fear death inasmuch as he is Word and God, but he was pressing on to carry the economy through to its end; for this is the will of the Father. ⟦q18.1|4⟧ But he has also the not willing to die, because the flesh naturally refuses death.» ⟦q18.1|5⟧ And this same [Father], commenting on the great evangelist John, says: [n: Joan. xii, 27.] «Christ himself made the discourse on this, teaching that dying for all he has as willed, because the divine nature had wished it; but as unwilled, because of the passions on the cross. ⟦q18.1|6⟧ And so far as it came to the flesh refusing death, he says such things.» ⟦q18.1|7+8⟧ And the inspired Severian, who was bishop of Gabala, on *Father, let this cup pass from me*, and on *Father, save me from this hour*: [n: Matth. xxvi, 38.] «The Lord, anticipating, stops the mouths of the heretics, to show that he put on this much-suffering body, the body that is in agony at death, that trembles at the violence of death, that grieves and is troubled at the end of life. ⟦q18.1|9⟧ He says: *Now is my soul troubled. ⟦q18.1|10⟧ My soul is exceeding sorrowful unto death*: not my Godhead; for the Divine is impassible and untroubled and unafraid. ⟦q18.1|11⟧ *For the spirit*, says the Lord, *is eager, but the flesh weak.* ⟦q18.1|12⟧ So he shows two wills: the one divine, the other human.»

⟦q18.1|13⟧ But I think that the account concerning the duality of the wills of the same [Christ] has been sufficiently shown by the God-bearing [Fathers]: both of one and another will, divine and human, and of death's being both willed and unwilled for the Saviour — the one on account of what he was from the beginning, the other on account of what he afterwards became. ⟦q18.1|14⟧ We must begin, then, also the account concerning the difference of the operations, and their duality, in order, with the testimonies of the God-speaking Fathers that set their seal on this one too.

⟦q18.1|15⟧ At once, then, the great confessor and teacher Ambrose, the archbishop of Milan, in his second book to Gratian, goes through these things: «Equal, then, in the form of God, but the same less in the assumption of the flesh and in the passion of the man. ⟦q18.1|16⟧ For in what way can the same nature be less and equal? ⟦q18.1|16⟧ And how, if it is less, does the same do likewise the things which the Father does? ⟦q18.1|17⟧ For in what way is the same operation from a different essence? [0168] For can the lesser operate as the greater does? ⟦q18.1|18⟧ Or can there be one operation where the essence is different?»

⟦q18.1|19⟧ And indeed the celebrated Cyril, hierarch of the Jerusalemites, in his discourse on the Gospel text where the Lord made the water wine, whose beginning is: «A wonder, and this too came about as a wonder. ⟦q18.1|20⟧ He wrought a wonder; he showed the twofold operation, suffering as man, operating as God, the same; for not one and another, even if in one way and another.» ⟦q18.1|21⟧ So also Leo, the all-strong and all-holy exarch of the great Church of the Romans, in the dogmatic tome to Flavian among the saints, against Nestorius and Eutyches of evil name: «For he operates in each form, with the communion of the other, what is proper to it; the Word working what is of the Word, the body carrying out what is of the body; and the one of them shines with the wonders, the other has fallen under the insults.»

⟦q18.1|22⟧ And John, who possessed the golden mouth, or rather Christ's, in his discourse on the Widow who brought the two mites into the Treasury, whose beginning is: «Simple is the name of fasting. ⟦q18.1|23⟧ And in other things the operation of the manhood of the conjoined natures is different, and the strength of the Godhead different. ⟦q18.1|24⟧ As I mean: below he toils, and above he holds the elements together. ⟦q18.1|25⟧ Below he hungers, and from above he supplies rains. ⟦q18.1|26⟧ Below he is afraid, and above he thunders. ⟦q18.1|27⟧ Below he stands at a tribunal, and from above he beholds himself. ⟦q18.1|28⟧ But in the matter of almsgiving, what belongs to the twofold operation runs together. ⟦q18.1|29⟧ For he who from above, from the Cherubim, awards prizes to the merciful, he, sitting before the Treasury, tests the lovers of man.» ⟦q18.1|30⟧ The same, in his discourse on Thomas the apostle, against the Arians: «Having heard these things, I cleansed my soul of unbelief; I stripped off the doubtful inclination, I took up conviction, I touched the body rejoicing and trembling. ⟦q18.1|31⟧ Together with my fingers I spread out the eye of my soul too, and at last I perceived two operations.»

⟦q18.1|32⟧ But indeed also the most wise Cyril, president of the Alexandrians, in the thirty-second chapter of the *Thesaurus*: «For surely we shall not grant that the natural operation of God and of a thing made is one; lest we either bring up what was made into the divine essence, or bring down the pre-eminence of the divine nature into [0169] the place befitting originated things. ⟦q18.1|33⟧ For those whose operation and power are invariantly one must also have the oneness of the genus preserved.»

⟦q18.1|34+35⟧ These things, then, these men proclaim piercingly, the Fathers of piety, whom, out of many, or rather countless, and out of the whole, so to speak in Scripture's words, cloud of witnesses, [n: Hebr. xii, 1.] we have brought forward cursorily, restraining the bulk of the letter, for the most evident demonstration of their true knowledge concerning Christ, the Saviour of the universe; impelled by which, they handed down to the holy Churches, moved by the Spirit, to hold that, just as the natures of the same and one are two, so equal in number to the natures are both his wills and his operations, and one and another volition and operation, divine and human, for the manifestation of the essential difference of the things from which, and in which, and which the same is; [a difference] which banishes the phantasm and the confusion together, and with them division altogether, as being made known in the one and the same God the Word, incarnate for us, [as the difference] of the things from which he really and unclouded is, according to the indissoluble union. ⟦q18.1|34+35⟧ For if the essential difference, both of the united things themselves and of what belongs to them naturally, is not made known without confusion in the utmost union according to hypostasis, neither will the principle of the union be made known without confusion.

⟦q18.1|36⟧ But those of the contrary and opposing party [say] the reverse. ⟦q18.1|37⟧ For Apollinarius the impious speaks thus in the discourse entitled by him *Demonstration concerning the divine incarnation in the likeness of man*: [n: Matth. xxvi, 39.] «And they do not remember that this will is said to be proper, not to a man from the earth, as they themselves suppose, but to God who came down from heaven.» ⟦q18.1|38+39⟧ And the same, again, the fool, in [the book] entitled *The incarnate manifestation itself of God*: «For Christ is one, moved by the divine will alone, just as we also know his operation to be one, proceeding in different wonders and sufferings from his one nature. ⟦q18.1|40⟧ For he is God incarnate, and is believed so.» ⟦q18.1|40⟧ And after a little: «And the [words] *Father, if it be possible, let this cup depart from me; nevertheless not mine, but thy will be done*, do not carry the reflection of one and another will, not concurring with one another, but of one and the same, operating divinely, but by way of economy refusing death; since he who said this was God bearing flesh, having no difference in willing.»

⟦q18.1|41⟧ And the disciple and successor of that man's impiety, and an enemy, true to his name, to the word of truth, Polemon the heretic, in his *Antirrhetic* against the holy Fathers, says these things perversely: «For the Word, the Christ, [0172] was God, and, united to the perfection of flesh and become man, not having mingled with himself the changeable mind, moved by natural will toward contraries, but rather having become mind to himself, he did all things by the unchangeable divine will. ⟦q18.1|42⟧ But not the one divine, the other deified, as Gregory the Cappadocian has it, since [that would be] changeable. ⟦q18.1|43⟧ For what could be deified could also in every way be made earthy, as the first Adam was.» ⟦q18.1|44⟧ And in the sixth of the letters written by him to Timothy, his fellow-worker and wicked accomplice in impiety: «He who says two wills of Christ, according to those who have said so of old and now, either brings in the one as two Christs, divided from one another not by nature only, but indeed by enmity also; or teaches that the same one is at war with himself. ⟦q18.1|44⟧ For where there is duality, there is in every way division.»

⟦q18.1|45⟧ But Themistius too, the shield-bearer of the faction of Severus and the leader of the folly of the Agnoetae, in chapter 45 of the second book of those against the tome presented to the empress Theodora by Theodosius, the heresiarch of the heretics named after him, [says] these things, hateful to God: «For not because the sacred Athanasius too said that Christ showed two wills at the time of the passion, shall we therefore also attach two volitions to him, and these at war with one another, according to these syllogisms of thine; but we shall know piously that the one volition of Emmanuel, as of one, moves now in a human way, now in a way befitting God.» ⟦q18.1|46⟧ And the same ill-met heretic again, in chapter 52, book 3, of the treatise composed by him in conformity with the impiety of his fellow-tribesman: «I say that the knowledge and the operation of Emmanuel are one, as also the volition. ⟦q18.1|47⟧ Consider, then, thus: he who is unchangeable, as God, he who is higher than every passion, moved in a manner befitting man according to the volition, refuses the passion; but again, in a manner befitting God, takes courage toward the passion; and each of these through flesh.» ⟦q18.1|48⟧ And these things these men [say] perversely.

⟦q18.1|49⟧ But those who are likewise opposed in mind to these and to the truth — I mean the leaders of division — being driven together into a wrong belief equal to theirs and the same, concerning one will and one operation, who also championed the union of inclination by relation, buzz these things about. ⟦q18.1|50⟧ Theodore, the evil-minded and contentious, who plundered [the Church] of the Mopsuestians, in the second book of what he misexpounded [0173] on the wonders: «*I will; be thou clean*, the Saviour, saying this to the leper, showed that the volition is one, the operation one, brought forth according to one and the same authority — not, I say, of nature, but of good pleasure — according to which the man who, according to foreknowledge, came to be afterwards from the seed of David was united to God the Word, having from the womb itself the inward appropriation toward him.» [n: Matth. viii, 3.]

⟦q18.1|51⟧ And the follower and successor of his madness, Nestorius the accursed, in what he calls the *Clear Initiation*, in the second book of the treatise on it, [says] these things maliciously: «We keep the natures without confusion, joined not according to essence but by inclination; on which account we see also their volition, operation and lordship as one, shown forth by equality of worth. ⟦q18.1|52⟧ For God the Word, having taken up the man whom he foreordained, was preferred by him in the principle of authority, on account of the foreknown disposition.» ⟦q18.1|53⟧ And the same madman again, in the same [treatise], book four: «God the Word was not one, and the man in whom he came to be another. ⟦q18.1|54+55+56⟧ For the person of both was one in worth and honour, worshipped by the whole creation, divided in no place or time by otherness of counsel and will.» ⟦q18.1|54+55+56⟧ Indeed Paul the Persian too, being a pseudo-deacon of the most foul heresy of Nestorius, in his discourse *On Judgement*, utters these things together with them, fighting against God: «Since the union of God the Word toward the man whom he took up did not come about according to essence, one nature did not come about. ⟦q18.1|54+55+56⟧ And if one nature did not come about, Christ is not one single-personed hypostasis. ⟦q18.1|54+55+56⟧ The union, then, is according to good pleasure, held fast by identity of counsel and inclination, so that both the difference of the natures may be shown unconfused, and the mystery of the good pleasure may be displayed by a monad of wish.»

⟦q18.1|54+55+56⟧ With these, as you see, all-excellent ones — examining both the writings and the doctrines before them — the Ekthesis, which now, I know not how, has crept in on account of our sins against the blameless faith, has proved very much of one voice and one accord in all things, ratifying the one will in Christ, and the one operation, like the senseless. ⟦q18.1|57⟧ The one will, by saying: «Whence, following the holy Fathers in all things and in this too, we confess one will of our Lord Jesus Christ»; and the one operation, by asserting: «But indeed to hold two wills also follows on this, that is, on the maintaining of the two operations.» ⟦q18.1|58⟧ For indeed if it determines that the wills follow the operation, it is in every way somehow necessary, the consequent having been ratified by it — I mean the one will — that the antecedent also be ratified, namely the one operation. ⟦q18.1|59⟧ For, hastening sophistically to bring this in together with the one volition, it decreed, as it saw fit, that the volition follows the operation. ⟦q18.1|60⟧ Therefore

⟦q19.1|1⟧ [0176] … and it knows as Fathers, whom it has followed in this and in all things, not those who are truly holy, but those who are not holy at all.

⟦q19.1|2⟧ For surely no one would ever say that Athanasius the celebrated spoke of one will, when he cries out expressly, as we have set out before: «He shows here two wills: the one human, the other divine.» ⟦q19.1|3⟧ Nor Gregory the Theologian, who says of the Saviour's human will: «For his willing is not even contrary to God, being wholly deified.» ⟦q19.1|4+5⟧ Nor his namesake, the teacher of the Nyssenes, who says: «The soul wills, the body touches»; and: «By the operating body, and by the impulse of the will that comes to be in the soul»; and: «Willing through the soul, touching through the body»; and: «The human will is one thing, and the divine another; and saying, Not mine, he signified the human by the word; but adding, Thine, he showed the conjoinedness of his own Godhead with the Father.» ⟦q19.1|6⟧ Nor John Chrysostom, who teaches: «For the words show not agony only, but two wills. ⟦q19.1|7⟧ And if what is said were about the Godhead, a certain contradiction arises; but if about the flesh, the things said have reason. ⟦q19.1|8⟧ For it is no ground of condemnation that the flesh does not will to die; for this belongs to nature. ⟦q19.1|9⟧ But he displays all the things of nature apart from sin, and with great abundance.» ⟦q19.1|10⟧ Nor Cyril of Alexandria, who wisely teaches: «For this was the will of the Father, to bring the economy through to its end. ⟦q19.1|11⟧ But he has also the not willing to die, because the flesh naturally refuses death.» ⟦q19.1|12⟧ And: «He has dying for all as what is willed, because the divine nature had wished it; but as unwilled, because of the flesh naturally refusing death.» ⟦q19.1|13⟧ Nor Severian, the president of Gabala, who testifies: «So that he shows two wills: the one divine, the other human.» ⟦q19.1|14⟧ But neither would anyone say that the great confessor Ambrose spoke of one confession, who prudently proclaims: «For in what manner is the same operation of a different essence? ⟦q19.1|15⟧ For can there be one operation where the essence is different?» ⟦q19.1|16⟧ Nor Cyril of Jerusalem, who charges: «He showed the twofold operation, suffering as man, operating as God, the same.» ⟦q19.1|17⟧ Nor the divine Leo, who declares with understanding: «For each form operates, with the communion of the other, what it has had as its own.» ⟦q19.1|18⟧ Nor Chrysostom again: «And in the other things the operation of the conjoined natures is different, of the manhood and of the Godhead; but in the matter of mercy, what belongs to the twofold operation runs together; and so I perceived two operations.» ⟦q19.1|19⟧ Nor Cyril likewise, the most sacred teacher of Alexandria: «For we shall surely not grant that the natural operation of God and of the thing made is one.»

⟦q19.1|19⟧ [0177] These, or some of these, it declares to be neither holy nor approved mystagogues of the Church; and it declares their glorious confession of two wills and operations to be impious, and alien to Christian doctrine. ⟦q19.1|20⟧ For it confirms the account for us, saying this: «And likewise the expression of the two operations scandalizes many, as having been spoken by none of the holy and approved mystagogues of the Church; and moreover there follows from it the professing of two wills, standing contrary to one another; and from this, that two who will contrary things are introduced; which is impious and alien to Christian doctrine.»

⟦q19.1|21⟧ Behold: plainly, and bare-headed, as the saying goes, it defines that the professing of two wills, and of the operations that on its account are their antecedents, equal in number to them, belongs not to holy men, nor to approved mystagogues of the Church, but rather to impious men, as impious and alien, as it says, to Christian doctrine; and as introducing two who will contrary things, for those who preach these things. ⟦q19.1|22⟧ That is: the two wills, and the operations equal in number to them, it charges to the Spirit-moved Fathers, whom it did not choose to follow, or to call holy, or at all to profess these things with them and after them, for the confirmation of the mystery of Christ God according to the flesh.

⟦q19.1|23⟧ But to whom, and who are those, concerning whom and by whom it said the expression «one operation» had been spoken, and whom it follows in this, as in all things, so as to confess the one will of Christ God — it has been shown both who they manifestly are, and that they are the champions of confusion and the leaders of division. ⟦q19.1|23⟧ For instance (for it is not out of place, for confirmation, to run over them again briefly): Apollinarius the impious, fighting against God thus: «For Christ is one, moved by the divine will alone, according as we know his operation also to be one, and having no difference in willing.» ⟦q19.1|24⟧ Polemon, the enemy of the truth: «With an unchangeable divine will he has made all things; but not the one divine, the other deified, according to Gregory the Cappadocian.» ⟦q19.1|25⟧ And: «He who says two wills of Christ, after those puffed up of old and now, either introduces the one as two Christs, or teaches one at war with himself.» ⟦q19.1|26⟧ Themistius the lawless: «But we know the one volition of Emmanuel, as of one, to be moved now humanly, now in a manner befitting God»; and: «I say that the knowledge and the operation of Emmanuel are one, as also the volition.» ⟦q19.1|27⟧ Theodore the God-stricken: «I have shown that the volition is one, the operation one, brought forth according to one and the same authority.» ⟦q19.1|28⟧ Nestorius the all-stricken: «Wherefore we see their volition, and operation and lordship, to be one.» ⟦q19.1|29⟧ Paul, a Persian in inclination too: «The union is by good pleasure, held together by identity of counsel and inclination»; and: «The mystery of good pleasure is displayed as of a singular wish.» ⟦q19.1|30⟧ These accursed and execrable men, then, it defines as holy Fathers. ⟦q19.1|31⟧ These it knows as approved mystagogues of the Church; and, following them in all things, and in this too, and defining with them one volition and operation of Christ God, it confuses and cuts asunder the principle of the economy just as they do.

⟦q19.1|31⟧ [0180] How then, thinking the things of its opponents, has it supposed that it thinks otherwise, setting the votes crosswise, and choosing and preferring non-being to being? ⟦q19.1|32⟧ For with truth, not injustice, as judge, it is surely plain to everyone that he is in harmony and agreement with them, not who says what they do not say, but who professes what they teach; since it knows to characterize what is of other doctrine by disharmony, and what is of the same doctrine by harmony. ⟦q19.1|33⟧ And yet it too bears witness in a way, crying that the foul Nestorius would never have dared to say two wills, but to confess identity of will, that is, one will, of the two persons fashioned by him. ⟦q19.1|34⟧ If then, even according to it, Nestorius professes not two wills but one; and Apollinarius too, and all the impious who come from them, and moreover one operation also, as the account has shown: then beyond dispute, by the things it teaches, it has set forth that we, who say two according to the divine Fathers, are entirely of other mind from them, and that itself, which says one, is of one mind with Nestorius and Apollinarius and those about them; and that it strikes out the divine Fathers, as I said, and enrols the accursed as its own Fathers.

⟦q19.1|35⟧ By what cause, or what kind of cause compelling him, has he brought it in against the pious confession? ⟦q19.1|36⟧ If on the ground that we had no faith, the account is false: for all who professed the right account were Christians even before it. ⟦q19.1|36⟧ But if on the ground that we had, the mode is one to be shunned, which brings in the superfluous as counterfeit; by which, overshadowing their own villainy, and having not one single testimony at all of any synod, or Father, or Scripture to bring forward in witness of their own views, they say these things, feigning the doctrines of piety, which were handed down to us by those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the Word, [n: Luc. I, 2.] and by their disciples and successors in order, the God-inspired teachers of the truth; which is the same as to say, the five holy and ecumenical synods of the most blessed and God-bearing Fathers. ⟦q19.1|37⟧ But if these handed these things down, what is the demonstration, or whence their confirmation of such doctrines? ⟦q19.1|38+39+40⟧ Besides, since we adhere to and confess the holy synods, it is plain that the invention of what has been brought in is counterfeit. ⟦q19.1|38+39+40⟧ But if these things are not of the holy synods, what is the bombast of this drama, which bends the ill-sounding under the name of the all-renowned, so that the appellation of the glorious Fathers and synods may be a bait for the simpler unto apostasy from the truth — an appellation ingeniously contrived from the very beginning by those of other [0181] mind, both for the covering of their own views, as I said, and as a kind of crafty snatching-away of those led astray?

⟦q19.1|38+39+40⟧ Hence, for the complete destruction of such men — I mean of those who at various times search out deceitful searchings against the faith — a synodal law too is most excellently defined by the holy assembly of the blessed Fathers at Chalcedon, enjoining somewhat thus: «The holy and ecumenical synod has defined that it is permitted to no one to bring forward another faith, that is, to write or to compose, or to think or to teach others; and that those who dare either to compose another faith, that is, to bring it forward, or to teach or hand on another symbol to those wishing to turn to the knowledge of the truth from Hellenism or Judaism, or from any heresy whatsoever — these, if they be bishops or clerics, the bishops are to be alien from the episcopate and the clerics from the clergy; and if they be monks or laymen, they are to be anathematized.»

⟦q19.1|41⟧ Who then, of those who have in any way perceived God, and who hang upon his all-radiant glory — from whom, and through whom, and to whom is the salvation of those who piously confess him — would still choose to abandon the orthodox faith handed down to us from above and from the beginning through the divine oracles and the Fathers, and to prefer the recent innovation; against which, as indeed against every other invented by those of other mind contrary to pious thought, the lawful sentence of the approved and synodal curse of the holy Fathers gathered at Chalcedon has been issued, as the account has shown? ⟦q19.1|41⟧ Unless perhaps, grown weary of his own life, he has preferred alienation from the glory that is from God.

⟦q19.1|42+43⟧ Wherefore, beholding it in the facts themselves, master, and perceiving that it is, plainly and openly, a forerunning and a proclamation — toward the overthrow of all godliness and the denial of the true knowledge of the Only-begotten — of the final error and of the last beast, according to the foretelling of the holy men who thought these things, from divine inspiration and most blessed illumination, for the guarding of us who have reached the ends of the ages: [n: I Cor. x, 11.] let us each watch this imported novelty with all the strength of his own heart, so that we be not carried away with it heedlessly, as it were, and carelessly, but stand very weightily and manfully against all impiety, casting down thoughts, to speak in Scripture's words, and every height lifted up against the knowledge of God. [n: II Cor. x, 4.] Hence too the Saviour of all himself, our Lord and God, securing us in his love for man: Then, he says, if any man say unto you, Lo, here is the Christ, lo, here, believe it not [n: Matth. xxiv, 23.] — sending the counterfeit and differing faiths and suppositions of the crooked concerning him very far from the mystery concerning him, and keeping his own followers from every alien opinion, by which [0184] those contentious and contrary-minded in manner are wont to trouble, and indeed to war against, the sincerity of the confession toward him; so that the pious and God-loving mind among us may never, caught by any of these, fall away from the truth, slipping aside by the persuasiveness of fables, and not made firm by the demonstration of the words of the Fathers. ⟦q19.1|44⟧ Watch then and pray, the Word again charges us for this reason, that ye enter not into temptation: [n: Matth. xxvi, 41.] wishing by watching to produce in us sobriety in this, and by prayer his succour according to grace. ⟦q19.1|45⟧ And he speaks here of the temptation that comes from error, not from necessity, into which we are led from within, not from elsewhere, turning aside from the straight and royal path.

⟦q19.1|45⟧ Cutting this straight yourselves, guided by God, guide wisely also those like me, your own, who limp on both hams, bringing them back to the shadowless and unsetting light of the most divine confession and conduct of the Word, looking to the recompense from there. ⟦q19.1|46+47⟧ Since a divine law also charges those strong, like you, to bear the burdens of the weak, and so to fulfil the law. [n: Rom. xv, 1; Galat. vi, 2.] And a heavy burden, beyond any other among hard things, is the indifference of words about the same matters, which arises in the more childish through the shifting of times and persons, by deceit perhaps, or by threat, of those who coax, fawning or being exacting, and who fasten on unrestrainedly, above all in a time of the disorder of the whole. ⟦q19.1|48⟧ Stretching out a hand in sympathy, then, to your suppliant, may you not cease, now cleansing him by word with knowledge, now strengthening him by prayer with love for man, and making him kin to, and bringing him before, God the Word, rightly worshipped and believed by you, and King of all the ages, both now and at his fearful appearing; to whom with the Father and the Holy Spirit be honour, might, glory, worship, unto the ages of ages. ⟦q19.1|49⟧ Amen.

⟦q20.1|1+2+3+4+5⟧ OPUSCULUM 16 — ON THE TWO WILLS OF THE ONE CHRIST OUR GOD

⟦q20.1|1+2+3+4+5⟧ *Of Maximus the great, the confessor: On the two wills of the one Christ our God.*

⟦q20.1|1+2+3+4+5⟧ Different shapes and forms have been devised by art by different men, for safety and adornment together; and by these they think to make a fine show in what appears, having grown weary, through folly, of what is hidden. ⟦q20.1|1+2+3+4+5⟧ But for thee, sanctified Father, who hast already transferred thy thought to the life without interval, virtue unartful, surpassing every form and shape, has sufficed for beauty and for guard; adorning, besides what is [0185] unseen, what is seen by all as well, so greatly as thou hast preferred to what is dissolving and to the world [worldly] a longing that stands firm and never has satiety. ⟦q20.1|1+2+3+4+5⟧ Or rather, showing thee, as is right, so far made akin to God and like him, as it has declared thee wholly estranged from matter and the things about it in relation, and unlike them. ⟦q20.1|1+2+3+4+5⟧ Hence too the being uncapturable by the things that act ill is thine. ⟦q20.1|1+2+3+4+5⟧ For he is not of a nature to suffer at their hands who by inclination has suffered the good things, and is wholly held fast by them, and has received the fulfilment of longing, the perfect victory in himself of what is longed for, and the cessation of movement, the ever-moving rest; according to which the death that long ago prevailed over nature vanishes, nature being no longer worsted by it through transgression. ⟦q20.1|1+2+3+4+5⟧ For thou no longer undergoest it again, because of the prevailing grace of the Spirit, by which thou art held fast through holding fast to it in prayers; and, accomplishing its paths with knowledge, thou showest in operation which are royal and divine for those who wish to walk straight on the unerring path of piety, and markest off the turnings-aside from these on either side; and for the one thou showest the threatened griefs, for the other the promised holy recompenses, so that by fear and longing thou mayest lead them up to the perfection that is in God.

⟦q20.1|6⟧ And admiring thy work, I fittingly praise thine understanding; or rather, struck by thy vigour in both, glorifying God who empowers thee and makes thee wise, and entreating thee to use the same methods toward those lacking in wits, and not to grow weary — for virtue has no weariness, being the accomplisher of all good things — until thou put into them the mind of Christ, [n: I Cor. ii, 16.] and train them to search out the depths of the Spirit, [n: ibid. 10.] whose very manifest things circumscribe all the wisdom and power of beings, and who reveals the wisdom spoken in a mystery to those who, like thee, have attached themselves to him and have judged nothing more precious than living with him.

⟦q20.1|7+8+9⟧ But since, possessing the virtue that is first of all and likewise last, as one that leads forward and as a seal shining round — I mean humility — thou hast deigned to inquire of thy servant and disciple, on account of the definition of natural will which the devout monk made, whether it is well or not, where he said that it «is a power appetitive of what is according to nature, and holding together all the idioms that belong essentially to the nature»: I suppose that it is well, and that this is one will and that of inclination another, and not out of tune with the teaching of the God-approved Fathers; even if it was thought by some not to be so, who [0188] insist that the Fathers define will as volition, and as the thing willed or what is willed.

⟦q20.1|7+8+9⟧ And who defines it so, and which of the Fathers, I would gladly ask them. ⟦q20.1|7+8+9⟧ For if so, what else is this but a circular demonstration, which does not distinguish the principle of each by itself, but sets down, against all likelihood, the same principle of each through the other, and puts it forward; which is what it is to define will by volition, and this again by that? ⟦q20.1|7+8+9⟧ For the things defined convert with their own definition. ⟦q20.1|10⟧ For that they call will volition too is plain. ⟦q20.1|11⟧ Yet they do not say this as a definition of will. ⟦q20.1|12⟧ For who can show it? ⟦q20.1|13⟧ Since then wish will be a definition of purpose, and movement in turn of motion, and manhood of man, according to those who say so. ⟦q20.1|14⟧ But whether they signify what is signified in this way or in that, they in no way harm its existence, whether what is indicated be a movement or an essence. ⟦q20.1|15⟧ For if this harmed it, the existence of all universals together with particulars would altogether collapse. ⟦q20.1|16⟧ For in all things we make use of different significations.

⟦q20.1|17⟧ And this too I say: that even if they call will volition, yet in no way do they call it the thing willed or what is willed. ⟦q20.1|18⟧ For how are aspiration and the object of aspiration the same? ⟦q20.1|19⟧ For if so, toward what will it be moved, being itself properly that very thing toward which it is moved, and not being in nature other than that? ⟦q20.1|20+21+22⟧ For it is a middle relation between the extremes, uniting them through itself, but not concurring with them in existence. ⟦q20.1|20+21+22⟧ And witness is the divine and great Gregory, who does not at all bring the thing willed and the thing begotten into identity with volition and generation, but through these, as natural relations, refers them back to the one begetting and willing. ⟦q20.1|20+21+22⟧ For if he did not even consent to make the reference of the thing willed or begotten to the volition and the generation — though volition is middle according to nature — «For it does not altogether follow, he says, how was he going to bring them into identity, and declare these to be one?»

⟦q20.1|20+21+22⟧ Besides, if they say that will is the thing willed, and we are by nature a thing willed and what is willed — for we are God's creature — then God has by nature no other will at all but us alone, coming to be and passing away, as we do; and before we were, he was bereft of all will. ⟦q20.1|23⟧ And the same will be concluded in our case too: a will proper to us and natural will not belong to us; only the thing willed from outside, being or not being, good or not such, will be wrapped around us. ⟦q20.1|23⟧ Moreover, the thing willed is something among the things outside. ⟦q20.1|24+25+26+27+28⟧ For it is called a thing willed and what is willed because of the one moved toward it by volition, and not because of itself. ⟦q20.1|24+25+26+27+28⟧ So that if he who has natural volition wills none of the things that are, there is for him no thing willed or what is willed. ⟦q20.1|24+25+26+27+28⟧ What account, then, have those who insist that the thing willed is will, or who declare that it is so called by the holy Fathers?

⟦q20.1|24+25+26+27+28⟧ [0189] But let it be said so, according to them; for our discourse is not about a difference of names, but about pious concepts. ⟦q20.1|24+25+26+27+28⟧ But let them answer this to us who fittingly ask: whether the divine will is other according to nature in relation to the human, and this other in relation to that, even if it be called and named in ten thousand ways. ⟦q20.1|24+25+26+27+28⟧ Let them teach this, and make firm our understanding, which is shaken over what is unknown; and let us not be much vexed at their impositions of names, but even contribute something of our own to them. ⟦q20.1|24+25+26+27+28⟧ For if it is not other and other according to essence, it is plain that it is one by nature and the same. ⟦q20.1|29⟧ And if this, the nature too is of necessity one and invariant. ⟦q20.1|30⟧ For where there is no natural otherness of wills, neither is there at all otherness of essence and nature. ⟦q20.1|31⟧ But if it is other and other by nature, they are altogether different; and if different, how must one not confess their number in quantity? ⟦q20.1|32⟧ For the denial of this works the utter destruction both of the difference itself and of the things that differ, as not being. ⟦q20.1|33⟧ For how is it possible both to be and not to be numbered, and for what cause? ⟦q20.1|34⟧ Or how are the wills, being according to nature, not numbered in the same way, if indeed the natures themselves would reasonably not cease from being numbered? ⟦q20.1|35+36⟧ For what is good in the case of those, since they are innate in the things and constitutive of them, ought to hold also for the things themselves; and either let them remove number from these too, as injurious according to them, or, as in no way harmful, let it be included in the case of those too, for the indication of the innate difference present in them, on account of which we use it even with the essences; or let them show how they do not altogether work the destruction or the confusion of the Saviour's natural will as man, by their refusal of number.

⟦q20.1|37⟧ And how is the Word incarnate perfect man, apart from natural will? ⟦q20.1|38⟧ For being deified by the union with God does not remove it from its true being according to essence, as neither the very nature of the flesh animated rationally and intellectually; just as the utmost and thoroughgoing commingling and union with fire does not remove iron from its own; but it undergoes the things of fire, since it has become fire by the union; yet it is heavy again according to nature, and cuts, because it has not suffered damage to its own nature, nor departed at all from natural operation; though it exists with the fire according to the same and one hypostasis, and does without interval both the things according to its own nature — I mean the cutting — and in turn the things according to the union, which is the burning. ⟦q20.1|39⟧ For the burning belongs to it, as the cutting also belongs to the fire, because of the utmost interpenetration and exchange of these into one another; and neither its nature — I mean the iron's — even though it is seen with fire, are we [0192] at all prevented from naming or numbering, nor its natural operation, even though it is [?] with burning, and has no interval toward it, but shows through and is known uniformly with it and in it. ⟦q20.1|39⟧ What reason, then, is there not to number what belongs naturally to the nature, that is, the will? ⟦q20.1|40⟧ And thereby to attest an imperfection in what is ours to God the Word made flesh, more than perfect and before perfection, although, by the good pleasure of the Father and the co-operation of the Holy Spirit, for our salvation, he shared equally in all the things of the nature, according to the union without interval, as indeed in the nature itself perfectly, save only sin; which was not even of the nature, but of an inclination, the nature having been moved contrary to its principle and its law: a deviation and a slip; [?]

⟦q20.1|40⟧ And to me the said monk seems fittingly to have attended to this above all, having distinguished the will of inclination from the natural. ⟦q20.1|41⟧ For the one, according to his definition, which is well made, is a power appetitive of what is according to nature. ⟦q20.1|42⟧ For every being whatever, and above all every rational one, naturally has appetite for what is according to nature, and, having received from God the power for this, has it according to essence, for its own constitution. ⟦q20.1|43⟧ For if it has not the appetite for what is according to nature, could it have it for what in no way is — whence and how — when that has no existence or movement at all? ⟦q20.1|44⟧ For only non-being is inert and without essence; and in no way is there any power of it at all among beings, or movement. ⟦q20.1|45⟧ But the other is self-chosen impulse, making turnings-aside to either side; and it is not distinguishing of nature, but properly of person and hypostasis.

⟦q20.1|46⟧ And having discerned this, the divided and man-worshipping Nestorius impiously taught a union of inclinations; so that he might confirm each hypostasis through the other, and the mere man might be preserved for him, having made the union with God the Word by a certain inclination and self-chosen movement, as he himself says; from which he also establishes the identity of will, or, to speak more properly, the multiplicity of will; inasmuch as, according to him, the union goes forward part by part at each movement of the will of inclination, from the imperfect to the complete, being borne along and advancing; and not from the ineffable conception itself, the Godhead of the Word having been united whole, perfectly, with all that is its own, to our nature whole and all that pertains to it, according to one and the same hypostasis.

⟦q20.1|47⟧ So then, that the said monk might set out precisely the completeness of the nature in God incarnate, and cast away what is opposed: the natural will he [0193] defined in him; the will of inclination he marked off, giving neither room to division, through its being at strife in this, nor entry to phantasy, through that natural will's not existing. ⟦q20.1|48⟧ But if someone perhaps insists that it is not possible for the two wills to be spoken of in his case otherwise than by opposition: if as different according to essence, I too accept it; but if as opposed, the account is false. ⟦q20.1|49⟧ For not whatever is different is altogether also opposed. ⟦q20.1|50⟧ For what is opposed is the work of an inclination moved, plainly, contrary to reason; but what is different, of a nature governed by reason; and the one is seditious of nature, the other manifestly constitutive. ⟦q20.1|51⟧ Essential difference, then, is for the constitution of the things in the nature; by no means opposition, which is for their dissolution. ⟦q20.1|52⟧ For nature does not have what is contrary to nature; nor is there any principle of what is at strife.
